METADATA: {"date":"2026-10-05","problem_id":"515"}
CLAIM: On 1,200 held-out file-transfer problems balanced between permitted and forbidden requests, with four files and four recipients, linear decoders of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct's final prompt-token residual state identify the requested file and its permitted recipient with at least 90% accuracy each, even among incorrect authorization decisions. Patching a fixed set of at most 12 attention heads from correct runs containing the same permission facts in reordered table rows corrects at least 30% of all initial errors while changing no more than 3% of correct decisions. Decoders, heads, and donor-selection rules are fixed on separate development data, with decoders trained on both correct and incorrect development runs; test names and permission assignments are unseen.

report:
# Decoding and repairing permission decisions in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Problem ID** | 515 |
| **Scenario** | Lack of adherence: Drift in long contexts, responses to knowledge conflict, incorrect tool use, bias |
| **Assessment Verdict** | +1 Likely feasible |
| **Likert Score** | +1 |
| **Confidence** | 0.82 |
| **Date** | 2026-10-05 |

## Bottom line
Matched Qwen tests demonstrate recipient decoding above 90% and nine-head repair above 30% with less than 3% disruption, leaving joint performance—not a missing repair mechanism—as the main obstacle. **+1 Likely feasible, confidence 0.82:** the component demonstrations favor achieving the claim within approximately three months, but different prompt distributions produced the successful decoders and interventions, so their combination remains unverified. [experiment_sc102] [experiment_sc6]

## 1. Introduction

> On 1,200 held-out file-transfer problems balanced between permitted and forbidden requests, with four files and four recipients, linear decoders of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct's final prompt-token residual state identify the requested file and its permitted recipient with at least 90% accuracy each, even among incorrect authorization decisions. Patching a fixed set of at most 12 attention heads from correct runs containing the same permission facts in reordered table rows corrects at least 30% of all initial errors while changing no more than 3% of correct decisions. Decoders, heads, and donor-selection rules are fixed on separate development data, with decoders trained on both correct and incorrect development runs; test names and permission assignments are unseen.

I read this as an existential claim that one development-fixed system must satisfy all six empirical thresholds on the same stipulated test set, with presentation, residual layer, identity-label mapping, and patch alignment left open.

1. Both identity decoders must reach 90% overall and separately among initial authorization errors: four criteria.
2. One fixed intervention using at most 12 heads must repair 30% of all initial errors and change at most 3% of initially correct decisions: two criteria.
3. Development/test separation, unseen names and assignments, and correct permission-equivalent donors must hold throughout.

Every part is needed; compatibility of successful decoding and repair on one problem distribution now decides the claim. For this scenario, success would distinguish retained permission knowledge from a faulty decision and show that a targeted intervention can restore adherence.

## 2. What the literature establishes

A **binding** is the association between an entity and its attribute—for example, a file and its permitted recipient. The closest literature supports both retained bindings during failure and sparse causal interventions, but its numerical results depend strongly on task and readout.

| Closest work | Published result beside the claim's thresholds | Relevance and mismatch |
|---|---|---|
| Propositional probes | On Tulu-2-13B, proposition-set exact match is 97% on templates, 55% on paraphrases, and 26% on Spanish translations; under template prompt injection, probes retain 98% while prompting falls to 7%. Claim: each identity readout ≥90%. | Strong evidence that correct relations can survive misleading outputs. The complete decoder combines token-level linear probes with a pairwise binding metric, rather than one final-token linear classifier. [lit_propositional_probes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19501) |
| Legible failures | Qwen2.5-7B Base wrong-trial binding accuracy is 27.6% (reported interval 23.6–34.5%) on eight choices. An independent four-choice replication across eight models reaches 47.4–79.9%, still below 90%. Qwen steering repairs 29% and preserves 79%, versus the claim's ≥30% repair and ≥97% preservation. | Closest published error-conditioned linear readout. Base versus Instruct, interference, and residual steering versus donor-head patching limit transfer. [lit_legible_failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11216) |
| Sparse Qwen head intervention | Eight candidate heads support a dynamic intervention that raises average Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct accuracy from 41.7% to 48.5%, or 61.3% with oracle error localization. Claim: one fixed set ≤12 heads with separate repair/disruption limits. | Direct support for sparse, model-specific correction, but aggregate accuracy does not establish either conditional intervention rate; heads are dynamically selected and ablated, not donor-patched. [lit_qwen_sparse_head_intervention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21214) |
| Fragile reasoning | On 60 selected perturbation-induced GSM8K failures, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct hidden-state patching repairs 0/60; residual steering recovers 7.2%. Claim: ≥30% repair. | Shows that a correct donor need not repair Qwen reasoning failures. Arithmetic generation and whole-state interventions differ from permission lookup and sparse-head replacement. [lit_fragile_reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01639) |

**The strongest published case for the claim** is the 97–98% template relation recovery, reinforced by the same-model sparse intervention gain. **The strongest published case against it** is the substantially sub-90% failure-conditioned binding readout, together with Qwen's 0/60 arithmetic patch recovery. These findings disagree about transfer, not about whether internal information and emitted answers can differ; the positive case wins for this bounded permission task once the matched component demonstrations below are included, but no paper settles the complete conjunction.

## 3. What the literature leaves open

Requested-file recovery and permitted-recipient recovery require different operations: copying the queried identity versus retrieving its associated permission. We evaluated both from original final-prompt-token states, including error-conditioned results, because the published binding accuracies do not settle either 90% requirement.

Sparse repair and preservation must be measured together, not inferred from an aggregate accuracy gain. Two experiments therefore applied the same frozen intervention to both initial outcome subsets; the remaining unmeasured result is all decoding and intervention criteria together on one test set.

## 4. What our experiments show

**Requested-file decoding.** With opaque identifiers, catalog-position labels, and a development-selected block-20 readout, accuracy was 1,175/1,200 = 97.92% (95% Wilson interval 96.94–98.58%). The same frozen decoder's descriptive error subset scored 123/125 = 98.40% (94.35–99.56%), exceeding both requested-file thresholds. [experiment_sc1]

**Initial recipient decoding.** A shared-stem-name presentation with the request before a reversed-column table, trained on 8,192 examples, reached 849/1,200 = 70.75% (95% assignment-cluster interval 67.85–73.51%). This substantial shortfall is evidence against easy recipient recovery, not a failed measurement. [experiment_sc2]

**Recipient decoding during errors.** With confusable names and a nonauthoritative history record, a converged development-selected decoder recovered 197/290 = 67.93% of initial errors (95% Wilson interval 62.35–73.04%), against 90%. It learned above the shuffled-label control but missed the claim by a wide margin. [experiment_sc4]

**Higher-data recipient decoding.** An independent presentation and split, 65,536 training examples, and a converged block-20 linear decoder produced 1,141/1,200 = 95.08% (95% assignment-cluster interval 93.86–96.27%). Its descriptive initial-error subset reached 300/309 = 97.09% (Wilson interval 94.56–98.46%); this demonstrates both recipient targets, although the changed data, presentation, and optimization do not isolate a single fix for the earlier shortfalls. [experiment_sc102]

**Semantically aligned head patching.** Eleven development-fixed heads, patched at corresponding prompt-token positions from the first correct reordered donor, repaired 112/123 = 91.06% of all initial errors (95% Wilson interval 84.69–94.93%). Only 2/1,077 = 0.1857% of initially correct decisions changed (0.05094–0.6746%), comfortably satisfying both intervention limits. [experiment_sc5]

**Final-token head patching.** Nine fixed heads with a maximum-correct-margin donor rule repaired 213/229 = 93.01% of all errors (95% Wilson interval 88.95–95.65%). They changed 0/971 correct decisions (interval 0–0.3941%); donors unavailable for some errors remained in the denominator, and this was an active repair intervention, not a preservation-only no-op. [experiment_sc6]

See Appendix A for experimental details and for runs that produced no measurement.

## 4b. In the News (non-academic sources)

**Concordance company blog, date not supplied; trust tier (news), self-report:** “Single model. All results are on Qwen3-30B-A3B. Cross-model transfer is untested.” This contextualizes interest in reading and modifying rule-compliance representations, but neither supports nor undermines the named Qwen2.5 claim quantitatively. [web_rule_compliance_representations](https://www.concordance.co/blog/reading-writing-rule-compliance-representations)

## 5. Why the claim succeeds or fails

**The claim becomes true if retained permission information and selective repair coexist on one presentation.** The decoders need only read original states; they need not themselves cause the patch's success. Thus the main compatibility requirement is shared task performance, not a new causal theory connecting probes to heads.

**Matched results overcome the literature's largest numerical gaps, but only component by component.** The higher-data recipient decoder clears 90% even on errors, while the nine-head intervention clears both repair and preservation limits by large margins. These are stronger evidence for this claim than Base-model binding or arithmetic-patching shortfalls, because they measure the named model on the stipulated permission task; they do not establish that either successful configuration inherits the other's capabilities. [experiment_sc102] [experiment_sc6]

**Recipient binding under a common prompt is the remaining technical driver.** The learned 67.93% error-conditioned result and the successful 97.09% result show that available information, label mapping, presentation, and decoder fitting matter materially. What still must hold is ≥90% recipient recovery on a presentation that also supplies useful reordered donors; the evidence has reached each side of that requirement, but not their intersection. [experiment_sc4] [experiment_sc102]

## 6. Assessment

**+1 Likely feasible, confidence 0.82, is the best estimate for approximately three months of relevant research effort.** Every numerical target has a working matched instance, and two independent sparse interventions demonstrate selective repair. Confidence is below a full-feasibility judgment because successful components were measured on different distributions, and recipient decoding also has substantial valid shortfalls. [experiment_sc1] [experiment_sc5]

**A joint held-out demonstration would move the score up; repeated joint trade-offs would move it down.** One development-frozen configuration meeting all six thresholds would justify +2 Feasible. Conversely, replicated matched results in which ≥90% recipient decoding consistently accompanies <30% repair or >3% disruption—or successful repair consistently leaves decoding below 90%—would weaken the compatibility argument and move the assessment toward balance or likely infeasibility.

### Why not the neighbouring scores

**The evidence favors +1 Likely feasible rather than either neighbour.** It is not +2 Feasible because the high-data recipient readout has not been evaluated alongside the successful head patches, and the low-data shortfalls caution against assuming transfer. It is not 0 Evenly balanced because the positive matched evidence now clears the recipient and coupled intervention thresholds, rather than merely suggesting their mechanisms; the earlier shortfalls do not outweigh those existential component demonstrations. [experiment_sc102] [experiment_sc6]

## 7. Limitations and further directions

The error-subset successes for both decoders were descriptive analyses rather than separate primary hypotheses, reducing their confirmatory strength without changing the observed finite-test counts. Synthetic identifier tasks and immediate binary decisions support the claim's allowed setup, not a broader conclusion about long-workflow adherence. Ground-truth-assisted donor qualification is permitted here, but does not establish a deployable authorization safeguard.

**Further directions**

- Train both decoders and select the head intervention on one development distribution, then freeze everything before a new balanced 1,200-problem evaluation. A six-criterion pass settles the outstanding conjunction.
- Repeat that joint evaluation with independently held-out assignment pools and name seeds. Stable margins would strengthen confidence; systematic incompatibility would lower the score.
- Compare the successful prompt formats on development data while measuring both recipient decoding and correct reordered-donor availability. This would identify whether presentation changes preserve both required capabilities rather than improve one at the other's expense.

## Appendix A: Experimental Details

### Common measured-experiment conventions

All six measured experiments used the released Hugging Face **Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct**, a 7B-class model with 7.616 billion recorded parameters, revision `a09a35458c702b33eeacc393d103063234e8bc28`, without weight updates or quantization. Inference used BF16, PyTorch SDPA attention, the native chat template, and complete untruncated prompts; each held-out test contained four files, four recipients, and exactly 600 permitted plus 600 forbidden requests. [experiment_sc1] [experiment_sc102]

Every file had one permitted recipient; recipients could repeat across files. Complete names and catalog-relative assignment vectors were disjoint across development/test. Linear classifiers used only one original post-block residual vector at the final nonpadding prompt token, before the model's terminal normalization; training-only coordinate scaling and an intercept preserve an affine decision function of that vector. All reported choices were frozen before testing. [experiment_sc2] [experiment_sc4]

Intervals below are 95% Wilson intervals unless marked **cluster**, meaning a percentile bootstrap over permission-assignment clusters. Percentages are empirical finite-test rates, not confidence-bound success requirements. Tables show the test endpoints and controls bearing on validity; classwise breakdowns and development sweeps remain in the result artifacts.

report:
# Decoding and repairing permission decisions in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Problem ID** | 515 |
| **Scenario** | Lack of adherence: Drift in long contexts, responses to knowledge conflict, incorrect tool use, bias |
| **Assessment Verdict** | +1 Likely feasible |
| **Likert Score** | +1 |
| **Confidence** | 0.82 |
| **Date** | 2026-10-05 |

## Bottom line
Published work shows that correct relations can remain internally readable during wrong answers and that sparse head interventions can improve Qwen's decisions. [lit_propositional_probes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19501) [lit_qwen_sparse_head_intervention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21214) **+1 Likely feasible, confidence 0.82:** for this bounded permission task, the favorable evidence outweighs the sensitivity of recipient retrieval to presentation and decoder fitting.

## 1. Introduction

> On 1,200 held-out file-transfer problems balanced between permitted and forbidden requests, with four files and four recipients, linear decoders of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct's final prompt-token residual state identify the requested file and its permitted recipient with at least 90% accuracy each, even among incorrect authorization decisions. Patching a fixed set of at most 12 attention heads from correct runs containing the same permission facts in reordered table rows corrects at least 30% of all initial errors while changing no more than 3% of correct decisions. Decoders, heads, and donor-selection rules are fixed on separate development data, with decoders trained on both correct and incorrect development runs; test names and permission assignments are unseen.

I read this as an existential claim that one development-fixed system must satisfy all six empirical thresholds on the same stipulated test set, with presentation, residual layer, identity-label mapping, and patch alignment left open.

1. Both identity decoders must reach 90% overall and separately among initial authorization errors: four criteria.
2. One fixed intervention using at most 12 heads must repair 30% of all initial errors and change at most 3% of initially correct decisions: two criteria.
3. Development/test separation, unseen names and assignments, and correct permission-equivalent donors must hold throughout.

Every part is needed; preserving recipient decodability while obtaining selective repair decides the claim. For this scenario, success would distinguish retained permission knowledge from a faulty decision and show that a targeted intervention can restore adherence.

## 2. What the literature establishes

A **binding** is the association between an entity and its attribute—for example, a file and its permitted recipient. The closest literature establishes useful mechanisms, but its numerical results depend strongly on task and readout.

| Closest work | Published result beside the claim's thresholds | Relevance and mismatch |
|---|---|---|
| Propositional probes | On Tulu-2-13B, proposition-set exact match is 97% on templates, 55% on paraphrases, and 26% on Spanish translations; under template prompt injection, probes retain 98% while prompting falls to 7%. Claim: each identity readout ≥90%. | Strong evidence that correct relations can survive misleading outputs. The complete decoder combines token-level linear probes with a pairwise binding metric, rather than one final-token linear classifier. [lit_propositional_probes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19501) |
| Legible failures | Qwen2.5-7B Base wrong-trial binding accuracy is 27.6% (reported interval 23.6–34.5%) on eight choices. An independent four-choice replication across eight models reaches 47.4–79.9%, still below 90%. Qwen steering repairs 29% and preserves 79%, versus the claim's ≥30% repair and ≥97% preservation. | Closest published error-conditioned linear readout. Base versus Instruct, interference, and residual steering versus donor-head patching limit transfer. [lit_legible_failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11216) |
| Sparse Qwen head intervention | Eight candidate heads support a dynamic intervention that raises average Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct accuracy from 41.7% to 48.5%, or 61.3% with oracle error localization. Claim: one fixed set ≤12 heads with separate repair/disruption limits. | Direct support for sparse, model-specific correction, but aggregate accuracy does not establish either conditional intervention rate; heads are dynamically selected and ablated, not donor-patched. [lit_qwen_sparse_head_intervention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21214) |
| Fragile reasoning | On 60 selected perturbation-induced GSM8K failures, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct hidden-state patching repairs 0/60; residual steering recovers 7.2%. Claim: ≥30% repair. | Shows that a correct donor need not repair Qwen reasoning failures. Arithmetic generation and whole-state interventions differ from permission lookup and sparse-head replacement. [lit_fragile_reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01639) |

**The strongest published case for the claim** is the 97–98% template relation recovery, reinforced by the same-model sparse intervention gain. **The strongest published case against it** is the substantially sub-90% failure-conditioned binding readout, together with Qwen's 0/60 arithmetic patch recovery. These findings disagree about transfer, not about whether internal information and emitted answers can differ; the positive case wins for this bounded permission task when weighed with the matched demonstrations below, while the negative case cautions against assuming that an arbitrary presentation will work.

## 3. What the literature leaves open

Requested-file recovery and permitted-recipient recovery require different operations: copying the queried identity versus retrieving its associated permission. We evaluated both from original final-prompt-token states, including error-conditioned results, because the published binding accuracies do not settle either requirement.

Sparse repair and preservation must be measured together, not inferred from an aggregate accuracy gain. Two experiments therefore applied the same frozen intervention to both initial outcome subsets; all decoding and intervention criteria together on one test set remain the next measurement.

## 4. What our experiments show

**Requested-file decoding.** With opaque identifiers, catalog-position labels, and a development-selected block-20 readout, accuracy was 1,175/1,200 = 97.92% (95% Wilson interval 96.94–98.58%). The same frozen decoder's descriptive error subset scored 123/125 = 98.40% (94.35–99.56%), exceeding both requested-file thresholds. [experiment_sc1]

**Initial recipient decoding.** A shared-stem-name presentation with the request before a reversed-column table, trained on 8,192 examples, reached 849/1,200 = 70.75% (95% assignment-cluster interval 67.85–73.51%). This substantial shortfall is evidence against easy recipient recovery, not a failed measurement. [experiment_sc2]

**Recipient decoding during errors.** With confusable names and a nonauthoritative history record, a converged development-selected decoder recovered 197/290 = 67.93% of initial errors (95% Wilson interval 62.35–73.04%), against 90%. It learned above the shuffled-label control but missed the claim by a wide margin. [experiment_sc4]

**Higher-data recipient decoding.** An independent presentation and split, 65,536 training examples, and a converged block-20 linear decoder produced 1,141/1,200 = 95.08% (95% assignment-cluster interval 93.86–96.27%). Its descriptive initial-error subset reached 300/309 = 97.09% (Wilson interval 94.56–98.46%); this demonstrates both recipient targets, although the changed data, presentation, and optimization do not isolate a single fix for the earlier shortfalls. [experiment_sc102]

**Semantically aligned head patching.** Eleven development-fixed heads, patched at corresponding prompt-token positions from the first correct reordered donor, repaired 112/123 = 91.06% of all initial errors (95% Wilson interval 84.69–94.93%). Only 2/1,077 = 0.1857% of initially correct decisions changed (0.05094–0.6746%), comfortably satisfying both intervention limits. [experiment_sc5]

**Final-token head patching.** Nine fixed heads with a maximum-correct-margin donor rule repaired 213/229 = 93.01% of all errors (95% Wilson interval 88.95–95.65%). They changed 0/971 correct decisions (interval 0–0.3941%); donors unavailable for some errors remained in the denominator, and this was an active repair intervention, not a preservation-only no-op. [experiment_sc6]

See Appendix A for experimental details and for runs that produced no measurement.

## 4b. In the News (non-academic sources)

**Concordance company blog, date not supplied; trust tier (news), self-report:** “Single model. All results are on Qwen3-30B-A3B. Cross-model transfer is untested.” This contextualizes interest in reading and modifying rule-compliance representations, but neither supports nor undermines the named Qwen2.5 claim quantitatively. [web_rule_compliance_representations](https://www.concordance.co/blog/reading-writing-rule-compliance-representations)

## 5. Why the claim succeeds or fails

**The claim requires a presentation that exposes both identities to linear readout while leaving decision errors amenable to a small, fixed intervention.** Passive decoding need not explain or control the repaired decision. Improving a decoder therefore does not itself create a new causal dependence between the readouts and the head patch.

**The permission-task demonstrations deserve more weight than the unfavorable cross-task precedents.** The successful identity readouts and active donor patches bear directly on the named model and task, whereas the published binding and arithmetic shortfalls concern different retrieval demands and intervention sites. Arithmetic patch failure remains a serious warning about transferring a repair method across tasks, but it does not negate a working permission-task intervention. [lit_legible_failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11216) [lit_fragile_reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01639)

**Recipient-to-label mapping is the technically difficult step.** Recovering a requested file largely requires tracking the named query; recovering its recipient additionally requires retrieving the bound attribute and translating it to a stable catalog label. The contrast between the low-data/history shortfalls and the higher-data readout success identifies decoder fitting and presentation as concrete research targets, rather than requiring a new model architecture or an intervention driven by probe predictions.

## 6. Assessment

**+1 Likely feasible, confidence 0.82, reflects attainability with meaningful sensitivity to configuration.** Working instances of the required components favor success, but the valid recipient-decoding shortfalls show that suitable representations do not automatically yield the claimed readout. Confidence rests on the proximity of the positive measurements to the stated task, tempered by this demonstrated variability—not on an unsuccessful or uncompleted replication.

**A joint held-out demonstration would move the score up; repeated joint trade-offs would move it down.** One development-frozen configuration meeting all six thresholds would justify +2 Feasible. Conversely, replicated matched results in which adequate recipient decoding consistently accompanies inadequate repair or excessive disruption—or successful repair consistently leaves decoding below its threshold—would weaken the compatibility argument and move the assessment toward balance or likely infeasibility.

### Why not the neighbouring scores

**The measured successes and shortfalls favor +1 Likely feasible rather than either neighbour.** The substantial recipient-readout failures, including a converged decoder that genuinely learned, make +2 Feasible too strong: transfer between admissible presentations is not routine. Conversely, 0 Evenly balanced would give those configuration-specific failures too much weight for an existential claim, because the higher-data readout and two selective donor interventions supply closer positive evidence than the unfavorable published comparisons.

## 7. Limitations and further directions

The error-subset successes for both decoders were descriptive analyses rather than separate primary hypotheses, reducing their confirmatory strength without changing the observed finite-test counts. Synthetic identifier tasks and immediate binary decisions support the claim's allowed setup, not a broader conclusion about long-workflow adherence. Ground-truth-assisted donor qualification is permitted here, but does not establish a deployable authorization safeguard.

**Further directions**

- Train both decoders and select the head intervention on one development distribution, then freeze everything before a new balanced 1,200-problem evaluation. A six-criterion pass would establish a complete working instance.
- Repeat that evaluation with independently held-out assignment pools and name seeds. Stable margins would strengthen confidence; systematic incompatibility would lower the score.
- Compare the successful prompt formats on development data while measuring both recipient decoding and correct reordered-donor availability. This would identify whether presentation changes preserve both capabilities rather than improve one at the other's expense.

Inference used BF16, PyTorch SDPA attention, the native chat template, and complete untruncated prompts; each held-out test contained four files, four recipients, and exactly 600 permitted plus 600 forbidden requests. Every file had one permitted recipient; recipients could repeat across files. Complete names and catalog-relative assignment vectors were disjoint across development/test. Linear classifiers used only one original post-block residual vector at the final nonpadding prompt token, before the model's terminal normalization; training-only coordinate scaling and an intercept preserve an affine decision function of that vector. All reported choices were frozen before testing. [experiment_sc2] [experiment_sc4]

## Bottom line
Combining a passive identity readout with a sparse head patch is a bounded compatibility problem, with recipient-to-label mapping—not a new repair mechanism—as the main risk. **+1 Likely feasible, confidence 0.82:** a relevant interpretability lab is likely to achieve the complete claim within the assessment's approximately three-month research window.

## 1. Introduction

> On 1,200 held-out file-transfer problems balanced between permitted and forbidden requests, with four files and four recipients, linear decoders of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct's final prompt-token residual state identify the requested file and its permitted recipient with at least 90% accuracy each, even among incorrect authorization decisions. Patching a fixed set of at most 12 attention heads from correct runs containing the same permission facts in reordered table rows corrects at least 30% of all initial errors while changing no more than 3% of correct decisions. Decoders, heads, and donor-selection rules are fixed on separate development data, with decoders trained on both correct and incorrect development runs; test names and permission assignments are unseen.

I read this as an existential claim that one development-fixed system must satisfy all six empirical thresholds on the same stipulated test set, with presentation, residual layer, identity-label mapping, and patch alignment left open.

1. Both identity decoders must reach 90% overall and separately among initial authorization errors: four criteria.
2. One fixed intervention using at most 12 heads must repair 30% of all initial errors and change at most 3% of initially correct decisions: two criteria.
3. Development/test separation, unseen names and assignments, and correct permission-equivalent donors must hold throughout.

Every part is needed; preserving recipient decodability while obtaining selective repair decides the claim. For this scenario, success would distinguish retained permission knowledge from a faulty decision and show that a targeted intervention can restore adherence.

## 2. What the literature establishes

A **binding** is the association between an entity and its attribute—for example, a file and its permitted recipient. The closest literature establishes useful mechanisms, but its numerical results depend strongly on task and readout.

| Closest work | Published result beside the claim's thresholds | Relevance and mismatch |
|---|---|---|
| Propositional probes | On Tulu-2-13B, proposition-set exact match is 97% on templates, 55% on paraphrases, and 26% on Spanish translations; under template prompt injection, probes retain 98% while prompting falls to 7%. Claim: each identity readout ≥90%. | Strong evidence that correct relations can survive misleading outputs. The complete decoder combines token-level linear probes with a pairwise binding metric, rather than one final-token linear classifier. [lit_propositional_probes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19501) |
| Legible failures | Qwen2.5-7B Base wrong-trial binding accuracy is 27.6% (reported interval 23.6–34.5%) on eight choices. An independent four-choice replication across eight models reaches 47.4–79.9%, still below 90%. Qwen steering repairs 29% and preserves 79%, versus the claim's ≥30% repair and ≥97% preservation. | Closest published error-conditioned linear readout. Base versus Instruct, interference, and residual steering versus donor-head patching limit transfer. [lit_legible_failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11216) |
| Sparse Qwen head intervention | Eight candidate heads support a dynamic intervention that raises average Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct accuracy from 41.7% to 48.5%, or 61.3% with oracle error localization. Claim: one fixed set ≤12 heads with separate repair/disruption limits. | Direct support for sparse, model-specific correction, but aggregate accuracy does not establish either conditional intervention rate; heads are dynamically selected and ablated, not donor-patched. [lit_qwen_sparse_head_intervention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21214) |
| Fragile reasoning | On 60 selected perturbation-induced GSM8K failures, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct hidden-state patching repairs 0/60; residual steering recovers 7.2%. Claim: ≥30% repair. | Shows that a correct donor need not repair Qwen reasoning failures. Arithmetic generation and whole-state interventions differ from permission lookup and sparse-head replacement. [lit_fragile_reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01639) |

**The strongest published case for the claim** is the 97–98% template relation recovery, reinforced by the same-model sparse intervention gain. **The strongest published case against it** is the substantially sub-90% failure-conditioned binding readout, together with Qwen's 0/60 arithmetic patch recovery. These findings disagree about transfer, not about whether internal information and emitted answers can differ; the positive case wins for this bounded permission task when weighed with the matched demonstrations below, while the negative case cautions against assuming that an arbitrary presentation will work.

## 3. What the literature leaves open

Requested-file recovery and permitted-recipient recovery require different operations: copying the queried identity versus retrieving its associated permission. We evaluated both from original final-prompt-token states, including error-conditioned results, because the published binding accuracies do not settle either requirement.

Sparse repair and preservation must be measured together, not inferred from an aggregate accuracy gain. Two experiments therefore applied the same frozen intervention to both initial outcome subsets; all decoding and intervention criteria together on one test set remain the next measurement.

## 4. What our experiments show

**Requested-file decoding.** With opaque identifiers, catalog-position labels, and a development-selected block-20 readout, accuracy was 1,175/1,200 = 97.92% (95% Wilson interval 96.94–98.58%). The same frozen decoder's descriptive error subset scored 123/125 = 98.40% (94.35–99.56%), exceeding both requested-file thresholds. [experiment_sc1]

**Initial recipient decoding.** A shared-stem-name presentation with the request before a reversed-column table, trained on 8,192 examples, reached 849/1,200 = 70.75% (95% assignment-cluster interval 67.85–73.51%). This substantial shortfall is evidence against easy recipient recovery, not a failed measurement. [experiment_sc2]

**Recipient decoding during errors.** With confusable names and a nonauthoritative history record, a converged development-selected decoder recovered 197/290 = 67.93% of initial errors (95% Wilson interval 62.35–73.04%), against 90%. It learned above the shuffled-label control but missed the claim by a wide margin. [experiment_sc4]

**Higher-data recipient decoding.** An independent presentation and split, approximately 65.54 thousand training examples, and a converged block-20 linear decoder produced 1,141/1,200 = 95.08% (95% assignment-cluster interval 93.86–96.27%). Its descriptive initial-error subset reached 300/309 = 97.09% (Wilson interval 94.56–98.46%); this demonstrates both recipient targets, although the changed data, presentation, and optimization do not isolate a single fix for the earlier shortfalls. [experiment_sc102] [compute_6]

**Semantically aligned head patching.** Eleven development-fixed heads, patched at corresponding prompt-token positions from the first correct reordered donor, repaired 112/123 = 91.06% of all initial errors (95% Wilson interval 84.69–94.93%). Only 2/1,077 = 0.1857% of initially correct decisions changed (0.05094–0.6746%), comfortably satisfying both intervention limits. [experiment_sc5]

**Final-token head patching.** Nine fixed heads with a maximum-correct-margin donor rule repaired 213/229 = 93.01% of all errors (95% Wilson interval 88.95–95.65%). They changed 0/971 correct decisions (interval 0–0.3941%); donors unavailable for some errors remained in the denominator, and this was an active repair intervention, not a preservation-only no-op. [experiment_sc6]

See Appendix A for experimental details and for runs that produced no measurement.

## 4b. In the News (non-academic sources)

**Concordance company blog, date not supplied; trust tier (news), self-report:** “Single model. All results are on Qwen3-30B-A3B. Cross-model transfer is untested.” This contextualizes interest in reading and modifying rule-compliance representations, but neither supports nor undermines the named Qwen2.5 claim quantitatively. [web_rule_compliance_representations](https://www.concordance.co/blog/reading-writing-rule-compliance-representations)

## 5. Why the claim succeeds or fails

**The claim requires a presentation that exposes both identities to linear readout while leaving decision errors amenable to a small, fixed intervention.** Passive decoding need not explain or control the repaired decision. Improving a decoder therefore does not itself create a new causal dependence between the readouts and the head patch.

**The permission-task demonstrations deserve more weight than the unfavorable cross-task precedents.** The successful identity readouts and active donor patches bear directly on the named model and task, whereas the published binding and arithmetic shortfalls concern different retrieval demands and intervention sites. Arithmetic patch failure remains a serious warning about transferring a repair method across tasks, but it does not negate a working permission-task intervention. [lit_legible_failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11216) [lit_fragile_reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01639)

**The next technical step is adapting the successful recipient readout to a presentation that also supports donor repair.** That requires keeping the retrieved recipient aligned with a stable catalog label as names and assignments change, rather than memorizing literal identifiers. Decoder training can include both authorization outcomes without changing the model or making the intervention depend on decoder predictions; the task-specific adaptation is therefore bounded, although not automatic.

## 6. Assessment

**+1 Likely feasible, confidence 0.82:** for the assessment's approximately three-month research horizon, a relevant lab is likely to achieve all six criteria with one frozen configuration. The work indicated by the evidence is adapting demonstrated permission-task readouts and donor patches to a common presentation, not discovering either capability from scratch. Confidence is restrained by the valid low-data and history-conditioned recipient failures.

**A joint held-out demonstration would move the score up; repeated joint trade-offs would move it down.** One development-frozen configuration meeting all six thresholds would justify +2 Feasible. Conversely, replicated matched results in which adequate recipient decoding consistently accompanies inadequate repair or excessive disruption—or successful repair consistently leaves decoding below its threshold—would weaken the compatibility argument and move the assessment toward balance or likely infeasibility.

### Why not the neighbouring scores

**The upper neighbour would understate the adaptation problem, while the lower would understate the available repair routes.** A converged recipient decoder still fell substantially short, so +2 Feasible would treat a demonstrated readout obstacle as routine. However, 0 Evenly balanced is too weak because selective repair was obtained with two different donor-selection rules and token scopes: the favorable intervention evidence does not rest on a single head-selection recipe.

## 7. Limitations and further directions

The error-subset successes for both decoders were descriptive analyses rather than separate primary hypotheses, reducing their confirmatory strength without changing the observed finite-test counts. Synthetic identifier tasks and immediate binary decisions support the claim's allowed setup, not a broader conclusion about long-workflow adherence. Ground-truth-assisted donor qualification is permitted here, but does not establish a deployable authorization safeguard.

**Further directions**

- Train both decoders and select the head intervention on one development distribution, then freeze everything before a new balanced 1,200-problem evaluation. A six-criterion pass would establish a complete working instance.
- Repeat that evaluation with independently held-out assignment pools and name seeds. Stable margins would strengthen confidence; systematic incompatibility would lower the score.
- Compare the successful prompt formats on development data while measuring both recipient decoding and correct reordered-donor availability. This would identify whether presentation changes preserve both capabilities rather than improve one at the other's expense.

## Appendix A: Experimental Details

### Common measured-experiment conventions

All six measured experiments used the released Hugging Face **Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct**, a 7B-class model with 7.616 billion recorded parameters, revision `a09a35458c702b33eeacc393d103063234e8bc28`, without weight updates or quantization. Inference used BF16, PyTorch SDPA attention, the native chat template, and complete untruncated prompts; each held-out test contained four files, four recipients, and exactly 600 permitted plus 600 forbidden requests. [experiment_sc1] [experiment_sc102]

Every file had one permitted recipient; recipients could repeat across files. Complete names and catalog-relative assignment vectors were disjoint across development/test. Linear classifiers used only one original post-block residual vector at the final nonpadding prompt token, before the model's terminal normalization; training-only coordinate scaling and an intercept preserve an affine decision function of that vector. All reported choices were frozen before testing. [experiment_sc2] [experiment_sc4]

Intervals below are 95% Wilson intervals unless marked **cluster**, meaning a percentile bootstrap over permission-assignment clusters. Percentages are empirical finite-test rates, not confidence-bound success requirements. Tables show the test endpoints and controls bearing on validity; classwise breakdowns and development sweeps remain in the supplied results. Seeds and checkpoint identifiers are reproduced exactly because they identify the experiment rather than estimate a quantity.

# Decoding and repairing permission decisions in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Problem ID** | 515 |
| **Scenario** | Lack of adherence: Drift in long contexts, responses to knowledge conflict, incorrect tool use, bias |
| **Assessment Verdict** | +1 Likely feasible |
| **Likert Score** | +1 |
| **Confidence** | 0.82 |
| **Date** | 2026-10-05 |

## Bottom line
**+1 Likely feasible, confidence 0.82:** working recipient readouts and active, selective donor-head repair on the stated task make the complete system a credible next step. The principal risk is preserving recipient-to-label mapping when the readout and intervention share one presentation, rather than obtaining either capability in isolation. [experiment_sc102] [experiment_sc6]

## 1. Introduction

> On 1,200 held-out file-transfer problems balanced between permitted and forbidden requests, with four files and four recipients, linear decoders of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct's final prompt-token residual state identify the requested file and its permitted recipient with at least 90% accuracy each, even among incorrect authorization decisions. Patching a fixed set of at most 12 attention heads from correct runs containing the same permission facts in reordered table rows corrects at least 30% of all initial errors while changing no more than 3% of correct decisions. Decoders, heads, and donor-selection rules are fixed on separate development data, with decoders trained on both correct and incorrect development runs; test names and permission assignments are unseen.

I read this as an existential claim that one development-fixed system must satisfy all six empirical thresholds on the same stipulated test set, with presentation, residual layer, identity-label mapping, and patch alignment left open.

1. Both identity decoders must reach 90% overall and separately among initial authorization errors: four criteria.
2. One fixed intervention using at most 12 heads must repair 30% of all initial errors and change at most 3% of initially correct decisions: two criteria.
3. Development/test separation, unseen names and assignments, and correct permission-equivalent donors must hold throughout.

Every part is needed; preserving recipient decodability while obtaining selective repair decides the claim. For this scenario, success would distinguish retained permission knowledge from a faulty decision and show that a targeted intervention can restore adherence.

## 2. What the literature establishes

A **binding** is the association between an entity and its attribute—for example, a file and its permitted recipient. The closest literature establishes useful mechanisms, but its numerical results depend strongly on task and readout.

| Closest work | Published result beside the claim's thresholds | Relevance and mismatch |
|---|---|---|
| Propositional probes | On Tulu-2-13B, proposition-set exact match is 97% on templates, 55% on paraphrases, and 26% on Spanish translations; under template prompt injection, probes retain 98% while prompting falls to 7%. Claim: each identity readout ≥90%. | Strong evidence that correct relations can survive misleading outputs. The complete decoder combines token-level linear probes with a pairwise binding metric, rather than one final-token linear classifier. [lit_propositional_probes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19501) |
| Legible failures | Qwen2.5-7B Base wrong-trial binding accuracy is 27.6% (reported interval 23.6–34.5%) on eight choices. An independent four-choice replication across eight models reaches 47.4–79.9%, still below 90%. Qwen steering repairs 29% and preserves 79%, versus the claim's ≥30% repair and ≥97% preservation. | Closest published error-conditioned linear readout. Base versus Instruct, interference, and residual steering versus donor-head patching limit transfer. [lit_legible_failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11216) |
| Sparse Qwen head intervention | Eight candidate heads support a dynamic intervention that raises average Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct accuracy from 41.7% to 48.5%, or 61.3% with oracle error localization. Claim: one fixed set ≤12 heads with separate repair/disruption limits. | Direct support for sparse, model-specific correction, but aggregate accuracy does not establish either conditional intervention rate; heads are dynamically selected and ablated, not donor-patched. [lit_qwen_sparse_head_intervention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21214) |
| Fragile reasoning | On 60 selected perturbation-induced GSM8K failures, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct hidden-state patching repairs 0/60; residual steering recovers 7.2%. Claim: ≥30% repair. | Shows that a correct donor need not repair Qwen reasoning failures. Arithmetic generation and whole-state interventions differ from permission lookup and sparse-head replacement. [lit_fragile_reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01639) |

**The strongest published case for the claim** is the high template relation recovery, reinforced by the same-model sparse intervention gain. **The strongest published case against it** is the substantially sub-threshold failure-conditioned binding readout, together with Qwen's arithmetic patch failure. Their numbers are juxtaposed above: these findings disagree about transfer, not about whether internal information and emitted answers can differ. The positive case wins for this bounded permission task when weighed with the matched demonstrations below, while the negative case cautions against assuming that an arbitrary presentation will work.

## 3. What the literature leaves open

Requested-file recovery and permitted-recipient recovery require different operations: copying the queried identity versus retrieving its associated permission. We evaluated both from original final-prompt-token states, including error-conditioned results, because the published binding accuracies do not settle either requirement.

Sparse repair and preservation must be measured together, not inferred from an aggregate accuracy gain. Two experiments therefore applied the same frozen intervention to both initial outcome subsets; all decoding and intervention criteria together on one test set remain the next measurement.

## 4. What our experiments show

**Requested-file decoding.** With opaque identifiers, catalog-position labels, and a development-selected block-20 readout, accuracy was 1,175/1,200 = 97.92% (95% Wilson interval 96.94–98.58%). The same frozen decoder's descriptive error subset scored 123/125 = 98.40% (94.35–99.56%), exceeding both requested-file thresholds. [experiment_sc1]

**Initial recipient decoding.** A shared-stem-name presentation with the request before a reversed-column table, trained on 8,192 examples, reached 849/1,200 = 70.75% (95% assignment-cluster interval 67.85–73.51%), against 90%. The trained readout exceeded its shuffled-label control, making this a valid recipient-decoding shortfall under an admissible presentation. [experiment_sc2]

**Recipient decoding during errors.** With confusable names and a nonauthoritative history record, a converged development-selected decoder recovered 197/290 = 67.93% of initial errors (95% Wilson interval 62.35–73.04%), against 90%. Its above-control performance establishes that the decoder learned but did not recover enough recipient identities. [experiment_sc4]

**Higher-data recipient decoding.** An independent presentation and split, approximately 65.54 thousand training examples, and a converged block-20 linear decoder produced 1,141/1,200 = 95.08% (95% assignment-cluster interval 93.86–96.27%). Its descriptive initial-error subset reached 300/309 = 97.09% (Wilson interval 94.56–98.46%); this demonstrates both recipient targets, although the changed data, presentation, and optimization do not isolate a single fix for the earlier shortfalls. [experiment_sc102] [compute_6]

**Semantically aligned head patching.** Eleven development-fixed heads, patched at corresponding prompt-token positions from the first correct reordered donor, repaired 112/123 = 91.06% of all initial errors (95% Wilson interval 84.69–94.93%). Only 2/1,077 = 0.1857% of initially correct decisions changed (0.05094–0.6746%), comfortably satisfying both intervention limits. [experiment_sc5]

**Final-token head patching.** Nine fixed heads with a maximum-correct-margin donor rule repaired 213/229 = 93.01% of all errors (95% Wilson interval 88.95–95.65%). They changed 0/971 correct decisions (interval 0–0.3941%); donors unavailable for some errors remained in the denominator, and this was an active repair intervention, not a preservation-only no-op. [experiment_sc6]

See Appendix A for experimental details and for runs that produced no measurement.

## 4b. In the News (non-academic sources)

**Concordance company blog, date not supplied; trust tier (news), self-report:** “Single model. All results are on Qwen3-30B-A3B. Cross-model transfer is untested.” This contextualizes interest in reading and modifying rule-compliance representations, but neither supports nor undermines the named Qwen2.5 claim quantitatively. [web_rule_compliance_representations](https://www.concordance.co/blog/reading-writing-rule-compliance-representations)

## 5. Why the claim succeeds or fails

**The claim requires a presentation that exposes both identities to linear readout while leaving decision errors amenable to a small, fixed intervention.** Passive decoding need not explain or control the repaired decision. Improving a decoder therefore does not itself create a new causal dependence between the readouts and the head patch.

**The permission-task demonstrations deserve more weight than the unfavorable cross-task precedents.** The successful identity readouts and active donor patches bear directly on the named model and task, whereas the published binding and arithmetic shortfalls concern different retrieval demands and intervention sites. Arithmetic patch failure remains a serious warning about transferring a repair method across tasks, but it does not negate a working permission-task intervention. [lit_legible_failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11216) [lit_fragile_reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01639)

**The next technical step is adapting the successful recipient readout to a presentation that also supports donor repair.** That requires keeping the retrieved recipient aligned with a stable catalog label as names and assignments change, rather than memorizing literal identifiers. Decoder training can include both authorization outcomes without changing the model or making the intervention depend on decoder predictions.

## 6. Assessment

**+1 Likely feasible, confidence 0.82:** a relevant interpretability lab is likely to achieve all six criteria with one frozen configuration over the approximately three-month assessment horizon. Confidence is restrained by the valid low-data and history-conditioned recipient failures, which show that linear readout quality cannot be assumed from the presence of permission facts alone.

**A joint held-out demonstration would move the score up; repeated joint trade-offs would move it down.** One development-frozen configuration meeting all six thresholds would justify +2 Feasible. Conversely, replicated matched results in which adequate recipient decoding consistently accompanies inadequate repair or excessive disruption—or successful repair consistently leaves decoding below its threshold—would weaken the compatibility argument and move the assessment toward balance or likely infeasibility.

### Why not the neighbouring scores

**The upper neighbour would understate the adaptation problem, while the lower would understate the available repair routes.** A converged recipient decoder still fell substantially short, so +2 Feasible would treat a demonstrated readout obstacle as routine. However, 0 Evenly balanced is too weak because selective repair was obtained with two different donor-selection rules and token scopes: the favorable intervention evidence does not rest on a single head-selection recipe.

## 7. Limitations and further directions

The error-subset successes for both decoders were descriptive analyses rather than separate primary hypotheses, reducing their confirmatory strength without changing the observed finite-test counts. Synthetic identifier tasks and immediate binary decisions support the claim's allowed setup, not a broader conclusion about long-workflow adherence. Ground-truth-assisted donor qualification is permitted here, but does not establish a deployable authorization safeguard.

**Further directions**

- Train both decoders and select the head intervention on one development distribution, then freeze everything before a new balanced 1,200-problem evaluation. A six-criterion pass would establish a complete working instance.
- Repeat that evaluation with independently held-out assignment pools and name seeds. Stable margins would strengthen confidence; systematic incompatibility would lower the score.
- Compare the successful prompt formats on development data while measuring both recipient decoding and correct reordered-donor availability. This would identify whether presentation changes preserve both capabilities rather than improve one at the other's expense.

## Appendix A: Experimental Details

### Common measured-experiment conventions

All six measured experiments used the released Hugging Face **Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct**, a 7B-class model with 7.616 billion recorded parameters, checkpoint revision **a09a354**, without weight updates or quantization. Inference used BF16, PyTorch SDPA attention, the native chat template, and complete untruncated prompts; each held-out test contained four files, four recipients, and exactly 600 permitted plus 600 forbidden requests. [experiment_sc1] [experiment_sc102]

Every file had one permitted recipient; recipients could repeat across files. Complete names and catalog-relative assignment vectors were disjoint across development/test. Linear classifiers used only one original post-block residual vector at the final nonpadding prompt token, before the model's terminal normalization; training-only coordinate scaling and an intercept preserve an affine decision function of that vector. All reported choices were frozen before testing. [experiment_sc2] [experiment_sc4]

Intervals below are 95% Wilson intervals unless marked **cluster**, meaning a percentile bootstrap over permission-assignment clusters. Percentages are empirical finite-test rates, not confidence-bound success requirements. Tables show the test endpoints and controls bearing on validity; classwise breakdowns and development sweeps remain in the supplied results.

report:
# Decoding and repairing permission decisions in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Problem ID** | 515 |
| **Scenario** | Lack of adherence: Drift in long contexts, responses to knowledge conflict, incorrect tool use, bias |
| **Assessment Verdict** | +1 Likely feasible |
| **Likert Score** | +1 |
| **Confidence** | 0.82 |
| **Date** | 2026-10-05 |

## Bottom line
**+1 Likely feasible, confidence 0.82:** the favorable evidence bears directly on permission lookup in the named model, rather than transferring results from unrelated reasoning tasks. Reliable recipient decoding is the difficult element, but the task-specific evidence provides a credible route to the complete claim.

## 1. Introduction

> On 1,200 held-out file-transfer problems balanced between permitted and forbidden requests, with four files and four recipients, linear decoders of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct's final prompt-token residual state identify the requested file and its permitted recipient with at least 90% accuracy each, even among incorrect authorization decisions. Patching a fixed set of at most 12 attention heads from correct runs containing the same permission facts in reordered table rows corrects at least 30% of all initial errors while changing no more than 3% of correct decisions. Decoders, heads, and donor-selection rules are fixed on separate development data, with decoders trained on both correct and incorrect development runs; test names and permission assignments are unseen.

I read this as an existential claim that one development-fixed system must satisfy all six empirical thresholds on the same stipulated test set, with presentation, residual layer, identity-label mapping, and patch alignment left open.

1. Both identity decoders must reach 90% overall and separately among initial authorization errors: four criteria.
2. One fixed intervention using at most 12 heads must repair 30% of all initial errors and change at most 3% of initially correct decisions: two criteria.
3. Development/test separation, unseen names and assignments, and correct permission-equivalent donors must hold throughout.

Every part is needed; preserving recipient decodability while obtaining selective repair decides the claim. For this scenario, success would distinguish retained permission knowledge from a faulty decision and show that a targeted intervention can restore adherence.

## 2. What the literature establishes

A **binding** is the association between an entity and its attribute—for example, a file and its permitted recipient. The closest literature establishes useful mechanisms, but its numerical results depend strongly on task and readout.

| Closest work | Published result beside the claim's thresholds | Relevance and mismatch |
|---|---|---|
| Propositional probes | On Tulu-2-13B, proposition-set exact match is 97% on templates, 55% on paraphrases, and 26% on Spanish translations; under template prompt injection, probes retain 98% while prompting falls to 7%. Claim: each identity readout ≥90%. | Strong evidence that correct relations can survive misleading outputs. The complete decoder combines token-level linear probes with a pairwise binding metric, rather than one final-token linear classifier. [lit_propositional_probes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19501) |
| Legible failures | Qwen2.5-7B Base wrong-trial binding accuracy is 27.6% (reported interval 23.6–34.5%) on eight choices. An independent four-choice replication across eight models reaches 47.4–79.9%, still below 90%. Qwen steering repairs 29% and preserves 79%, versus the claim's ≥30% repair and ≥97% preservation. | Closest published error-conditioned linear readout. Base versus Instruct, interference, and residual steering versus donor-head patching limit transfer. [lit_legible_failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11216) |
| Sparse Qwen head intervention | Eight candidate heads support a dynamic intervention that raises average Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct accuracy from 41.7% to 48.5%, or 61.3% with oracle error localization. Claim: one fixed set ≤12 heads with separate repair/disruption limits. | Direct support for sparse, model-specific correction, but aggregate accuracy does not establish either conditional intervention rate; heads are dynamically selected and ablated, not donor-patched. [lit_qwen_sparse_head_intervention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21214) |
| Fragile reasoning | On 60 selected perturbation-induced GSM8K failures, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct hidden-state patching repairs 0/60; residual steering recovers 7.2%. Claim: ≥30% repair. | Shows that a correct donor need not repair Qwen reasoning failures. Arithmetic generation and whole-state interventions differ from permission lookup and sparse-head replacement. [lit_fragile_reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01639) |

**The strongest published case for the claim** is the high template relation recovery, reinforced by the same-model sparse intervention gain. **The strongest published case against it** is the substantially sub-threshold failure-conditioned binding readout, together with Qwen's arithmetic patch failure. Their numbers are juxtaposed above: these findings disagree about transfer, not about whether internal information and emitted answers can differ. The positive case wins for this bounded permission task when weighed with the matched demonstrations below, while the negative case cautions against assuming that an arbitrary presentation will work.

## 3. What the literature leaves open

Requested-file recovery and permitted-recipient recovery require different operations: copying the queried identity versus retrieving its associated permission. We evaluated both from original final-prompt-token states, including error-conditioned results, because the published binding accuracies do not settle either requirement.

Sparse repair and preservation must be measured together, not inferred from an aggregate accuracy gain. Two experiments therefore applied the same frozen intervention to both initial outcome subsets; all decoding and intervention criteria together on one test set remain the next measurement.

## 4. What our experiments show

**Requested-file decoding.** With opaque identifiers, catalog-position labels, and a development-selected block-20 readout, accuracy was 1,175/1,200 = 97.92% (95% Wilson interval 96.94–98.58%). The same frozen decoder's descriptive error subset scored 123/125 = 98.40% (94.35–99.56%), exceeding both requested-file thresholds. [experiment_sc1]

**Initial recipient decoding.** This experiment used a development-selected shared-stem-name prompt with the request before a reversed-column table and trained a linear readout on 8,192 examples. It recovered 849/1,200 = 70.75% (95% assignment-cluster interval 67.85–73.51%), against 90%. [experiment_sc2]

**Recipient decoding during errors.** A converged development-selected decoder used confusable names and a nonauthoritative history record. It recovered 197/290 = 67.93% of initial authorization errors (95% Wilson interval 62.35–73.04%), against 90%. [experiment_sc4]

**Higher-data recipient decoding.** An independent presentation and split, approximately 65.54 thousand training examples, and a converged block-20 linear decoder produced 1,141/1,200 = 95.08% (95% assignment-cluster interval 93.86–96.27%). Its descriptive initial-error subset reached 300/309 = 97.09% (Wilson interval 94.56–98.46%); this demonstrates both recipient targets, although the changed data, presentation, and optimization do not isolate a single fix for the earlier shortfalls. [experiment_sc102] [compute_6]

**Semantically aligned head patching.** Eleven development-fixed heads, patched at corresponding prompt-token positions from the first correct reordered donor, repaired 112/123 = 91.06% of all initial errors (95% Wilson interval 84.69–94.93%). Only 2/1,077 = 0.1857% of initially correct decisions changed (0.05094–0.6746%), comfortably satisfying both intervention limits. [experiment_sc5]

**Final-token head patching.** Nine fixed heads with a maximum-correct-margin donor rule repaired 213/229 = 93.01% of all errors (95% Wilson interval 88.95–95.65%). They changed 0/971 correct decisions (interval 0–0.3941%); donors unavailable for some errors remained in the denominator, and this was an active repair intervention, not a preservation-only no-op. [experiment_sc6]

See Appendix A for experimental details and for runs that produced no measurement.

## 4b. In the News (non-academic sources)

**Concordance company blog, date not supplied; trust tier (news), self-report:** “Single model. All results are on Qwen3-30B-A3B. Cross-model transfer is untested.” This contextualizes interest in reading and modifying rule-compliance representations, but neither supports nor undermines the named Qwen2.5 claim quantitatively. [web_rule_compliance_representations](https://www.concordance.co/blog/reading-writing-rule-compliance-representations)

## 5. Why the claim succeeds or fails

**The claim requires a presentation that exposes both identities to linear readout while leaving decision errors amenable to a small, fixed intervention.** Passive decoding need not explain or control the repaired decision. Improving a decoder therefore does not itself create a new causal dependence between the readouts and the head patch.

**The permission-task demonstrations deserve more weight than the unfavorable cross-task precedents.** The successful identity readouts and active donor patches bear directly on the named model and task, whereas the published binding and arithmetic shortfalls concern different retrieval demands and intervention sites. Arithmetic patch failure remains a serious warning about transferring a repair method across tasks, but it does not negate a working permission-task intervention. [lit_legible_failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11216) [lit_fragile_reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01639)

**The next technical step is adapting the successful recipient readout to a presentation that also supports donor repair.** That requires keeping the retrieved recipient aligned with a stable catalog label as names and assignments change, rather than memorizing literal identifiers. Decoder training can include both authorization outcomes without changing the model or making the intervention depend on decoder predictions.

## 6. Assessment

**+1 Likely feasible, confidence 0.82:** a relevant interpretability lab is likely to achieve all six criteria with one frozen configuration over the approximately three-month assessment horizon. Confidence is restrained by the valid low-data and history-conditioned recipient failures, which show that linear readout quality cannot be assumed from the presence of permission facts alone.

**A complete held-out result would settle whether the successful components are compatible.** One development-frozen configuration meeting all six thresholds would move the score to +2 Feasible. Conversely, replicated matched results in which adequate recipient decoding consistently accompanies inadequate repair or excessive disruption—or successful repair consistently leaves decoding below its threshold—would move the assessment toward balance or likely infeasibility.

### Why not the neighbouring scores

**The upper neighbour would understate the adaptation problem, while the lower would understate the available repair routes.** A converged recipient decoder still fell substantially short, so +2 Feasible would treat a demonstrated readout obstacle as routine. However, 0 Evenly balanced is too weak because selective repair was obtained with two different donor-selection rules and token scopes: the favorable intervention evidence does not rest on a single head-selection recipe.

## 7. Limitations and further directions

The error-subset successes for both decoders were descriptive analyses rather than separate primary hypotheses, reducing their confirmatory strength without changing the observed finite-test counts. Synthetic identifier tasks and immediate binary decisions support the claim's allowed setup, not a broader conclusion about long-workflow adherence. Ground-truth-assisted donor qualification is permitted here, but does not establish a deployable authorization safeguard.

**Further directions**

- Train both decoders and select the head intervention on one development distribution, then freeze everything before a new balanced 1,200-problem evaluation. A six-criterion pass would establish a complete working instance.
- Repeat that evaluation with independently held-out assignment pools and name seeds. Stable margins would strengthen confidence; systematic incompatibility would lower the score.
- Compare the successful prompt formats on development data while measuring both recipient decoding and correct reordered-donor availability. This would identify whether presentation changes preserve both capabilities rather than improve one at the other's expense.

## Appendix A: Experimental Details

### Common measured-experiment conventions

All six measured experiments used the released Hugging Face **Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct**, a 7B-class model with 7.616 billion recorded parameters, checkpoint revision **a09a354**, without weight updates or quantization. Inference used BF16, PyTorch SDPA attention, the native chat template, and complete untruncated prompts; each held-out test contained four files, four recipients, and exactly 600 permitted plus 600 forbidden requests. [experiment_sc1] [experiment_sc102]

Every file had one permitted recipient; recipients could repeat across files. Complete names and catalog-relative assignment vectors were disjoint across development/test. Linear classifiers used only one original post-block residual vector at the final nonpadding prompt token, before the model's terminal normalization; training-only coordinate scaling and an intercept preserve an affine decision function of that vector. All reported choices were frozen before testing. [experiment_sc2] [experiment_sc4]

Intervals below are 95% Wilson intervals unless marked **cluster**, meaning a percentile bootstrap over permission-assignment clusters. Percentages are empirical finite-test rates, not confidence-bound success requirements. Tables show the test endpoints and controls bearing on validity; classwise breakdowns and development sweeps remain in the supplied results.

### A.1 Requested-file readout

**Target:** ≥1,080/1,200 overall requested-file predictions and ≥90% among initial errors; a lower measured rate would be a shortfall for this configuration. **Data:** FourFileTransfer-Generated-v1, with 1,024 pilot, 4,096 fitting, 1,024 selection, 640 separate positive-control, and 1,200 test problems; recipient-rotation orbits allocated 128 permission vectors each to development and test. Fitting included 3,691 correct and 405 incorrect authorization runs. [experiment_sc1]
