report:
# Decoding and repairing permission decisions in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Problem ID** | 515 |
| **Scenario** | Lack of adherence: Drift in long contexts, responses to knowledge conflict, incorrect tool use, bias |
| **Assessment Verdict** | +1 Likely feasible |
| **Likert Score** | +1 |
| **Confidence** | 0.82 |
| **Date** | 2026-10-05 |

## Bottom line
**+1 Likely feasible, confidence 0.82:** separate four-file/four-recipient tests of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct achieved 95.08% recipient decoding and nine-head repair of 93.01% of initial errors with no observed changes to initially correct decisions. The donor intervention changes the computation while preserving the permission facts, demonstrating selective repair rather than only a correlation between internal states and errors.

## 1. Introduction

> On 1,200 held-out file-transfer problems balanced between permitted and forbidden requests, with four files and four recipients, linear decoders of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct's final prompt-token residual state identify the requested file and its permitted recipient with at least 90% accuracy each, even among incorrect authorization decisions. Patching a fixed set of at most 12 attention heads from correct runs containing the same permission facts in reordered table rows corrects at least 30% of all initial errors while changing no more than 3% of correct decisions. Decoders, heads, and donor-selection rules are fixed on separate development data, with decoders trained on both correct and incorrect development runs; test names and permission assignments are unseen.

I read this as an existential claim that one development-fixed system must satisfy all six empirical thresholds on the same stipulated test set, with presentation, residual layer, identity-label mapping, and patch alignment left open.

1. Both identity decoders must reach 90% overall and separately among initial authorization errors: four criteria.
2. One fixed intervention using at most 12 heads must repair 30% of all initial errors and change at most 3% of initially correct decisions: two criteria.
3. Development/test separation, unseen names and assignments, and correct permission-equivalent donors must hold throughout.

Every part is needed; preserving recipient decodability while obtaining selective repair decides the claim. For this scenario, success would distinguish retained permission knowledge from a faulty decision and show that a targeted intervention can restore adherence.

## 2. What the literature establishes

A **binding** is the association between an entity and its attribute—for example, a file and its permitted recipient. The closest literature establishes useful mechanisms, but its numerical results depend strongly on task and readout.

| Closest work | Published result beside the claim's thresholds | Relevance and mismatch |
|---|---|---|
| Propositional probes | On Tulu-2-13B, proposition-set exact match is 97% on templates, 55% on paraphrases, and 26% on Spanish translations; under template prompt injection, probes retain 98% while prompting falls to 7%. Claim: each identity readout ≥90%. | Strong evidence that correct relations can survive misleading outputs. The complete decoder combines token-level linear probes with comparisons between entity and attribute token states to recover their association, rather than one final-token linear classifier. [lit_propositional_probes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19501) |
| Legible failures | Qwen2.5-7B Base wrong-trial binding accuracy is 27.6% (reported interval 23.6–34.5%) on eight choices. The paper's independent replication in its section 3.3 reports four-choice failure-conditioned accuracy of 47.4–79.9% across eight models, still below 90%. Qwen steering repairs 29% and preserves 79%, versus the claim's ≥30% repair and ≥97% preservation. | Closest published error-conditioned linear readout. Base versus Instruct, interference, and residual steering versus donor-head patching limit transfer. [lit_legible_failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11216) |
| Sparse Qwen head intervention | Eight candidate heads support a dynamic intervention that raises average Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct accuracy from 41.7% to 48.5%, or 61.3% when given the locations of erroneous predictions. Claim: one fixed set ≤12 heads with separate repair/disruption limits. | Direct support for sparse, model-specific correction, but aggregate accuracy does not establish either conditional intervention rate; heads are dynamically selected and ablated, not donor-patched. [lit_qwen_sparse_head_intervention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21214) |
| Fragile reasoning | On 60 selected perturbation-induced GSM8K failures, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct hidden-state patching repairs 0/60; residual steering recovers 7.2%. Claim: ≥30% repair. | Shows that a correct donor need not repair Qwen reasoning failures. Arithmetic generation and whole-state interventions differ from permission lookup and sparse-head replacement. [lit_fragile_reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01639) |

**The strongest published case for the claim** is the high template relation recovery, reinforced by the same-model sparse intervention gain. **The strongest published case against it** is the substantially sub-threshold failure-conditioned binding readout, together with Qwen's arithmetic patch failure. Their numbers are juxtaposed above: these findings disagree about transfer, not about whether internal information and emitted answers can differ. The positive case wins for this bounded permission task when weighed with the matched demonstrations below, while the negative case cautions against assuming that an arbitrary presentation will work.

## 3. What the literature leaves open

Requested-file recovery and permitted-recipient recovery require different operations: copying the queried identity versus retrieving its associated permission. We evaluated both from original final-prompt-token states, including error-conditioned results, because the published binding accuracies do not settle either requirement.

Sparse repair and preservation must be measured together, not inferred from an aggregate accuracy gain. Two experiments therefore applied the same frozen intervention to both initial outcome subsets; all decoding and intervention criteria together on one test set remain the next measurement.

## 4. What our experiments show

**Requested-file decoding.** With opaque identifiers, catalog-position labels, and a development-selected block-20 readout, accuracy was 1,175/1,200 = 97.92% (95% Wilson interval 96.94–98.58%, a confidence interval for a binomial proportion). The same frozen decoder's descriptive error subset scored 123/125 = 98.40% (94.35–99.56%), exceeding both requested-file thresholds.

**Initial recipient decoding—shared-stem names, request before a reversed-column table, and 8,192 training examples.** The frozen linear readout recovered 849/1,200 = 70.75% (95% interval 67.85–73.51%, calculated by resampling permission assignments), against 90%.

**Recipient decoding during errors—confusable names, an inactive history record, and a converged linear readout.** Accuracy was 197/290 = 67.93% over initial authorization errors (95% Wilson interval 62.35–73.04%), against 90%.

**Higher-data recipient decoding.** An independent presentation and split, approximately 65.54 thousand training examples, and a converged block-20 linear decoder produced 1,141/1,200 = 95.08% (95% interval 93.86–96.27%, calculated by resampling permission assignments). Its descriptive initial-error subset reached 300/309 = 97.09% (Wilson interval 94.56–98.46%); this demonstrates both recipient targets, although the changed data, presentation, and optimization do not isolate a single fix for the earlier shortfalls.

**Semantically aligned head patching.** Eleven development-fixed heads, patched at corresponding prompt-token positions from the first correct reordered donor, repaired 112/123 = 91.06% of all initial errors (95% Wilson interval 84.69–94.93%). Only 2/1,077 = 0.1857% of initially correct decisions changed (0.05094–0.6746%), comfortably satisfying both intervention limits.

**Final-token head patching.** Nine fixed heads with a maximum-correct-margin donor rule repaired 213/229 = 93.01% of all errors (95% Wilson interval 88.95–95.65%). They changed 0/971 correct decisions (interval 0–0.3941%); donors unavailable for some errors remained in the denominator, and this was an active repair intervention, not a preservation-only no-op.

See Appendix A for experimental details and for runs that produced no measurement.

## 4b. In the News (non-academic sources)

**Concordance company blog, date not supplied; trust tier (news), self-report:** “Single model. All results are on Qwen3-30B-A3B. Cross-model transfer is untested.” This contextualizes interest in reading and modifying rule-compliance representations, but neither supports nor undermines the named Qwen2.5 claim quantitatively. [web_rule_compliance_representations](https://www.concordance.co/blog/reading-writing-rule-compliance-representations)

## 5. Why the claim succeeds or fails

**The claim requires readable identities and selective repair to coexist on one presentation.** The intervention need not use the probe's predictions, so the two methods can be optimized separately before their joint evaluation.

**The permission-task demonstrations are the decisive evidence.** The higher-data recipient run and the nine-head donor-patch run establish working capabilities in the named model under the claim's conditions, whereas the unfavorable published binding and arithmetic results measure different retrieval demands and intervention sites. [experiment_sc102] [experiment_sc6] [lit_legible_failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11216) [lit_fragile_reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01639)

**The next technical step is adapting the successful recipient readout to a presentation that also supports donor repair.** That requires keeping the retrieved recipient aligned with a stable catalog label as names and assignments change, rather than memorizing literal identifiers.

## 6. Assessment

**For the approximately three-month feasibility assessment, a relevant interpretability lab is likely to achieve all six criteria with one frozen configuration.** Confidence of 0.82 is limited by using one fixed set of random seeds per experiment, which measures only those configurations rather than variability across fresh data draws.

**A development-frozen six-criterion pass would move the score to +2 Feasible.** Conversely, replicated matched results in which adequate recipient decoding consistently accompanies inadequate repair or excessive disruption—or successful repair consistently leaves decoding below its threshold—would move the assessment toward balance or likely infeasibility.

### Why not the neighbouring scores

**+2 Feasible would overstate the evidence, because the successful readout and the selective repair were measured in separate experiments and no single development-frozen system has yet met all six criteria together.** 0 Evenly balanced would discount the diversity of successful repair: two donor-selection rules and token scopes worked, so the positive case does not depend on one head-selection recipe.

## 7. Limitations and further directions

The error-subset successes for both decoders were descriptive analyses rather than separate primary hypotheses, reducing their confirmatory strength without changing the observed finite-test counts. Synthetic identifier tasks and immediate binary decisions support the claim's allowed setup, not a broader conclusion about long-workflow adherence. Ground-truth-assisted donor qualification is permitted here, but does not establish a deployable authorization safeguard.

**Further directions**

- Train both decoders and select the head intervention on one development distribution, then freeze everything before a new balanced 1,200-problem evaluation. A six-criterion pass would establish a complete working instance.
- Repeat that evaluation with independently held-out assignment pools and name seeds. Stable margins would strengthen confidence; systematic incompatibility would lower the score.
- Compare the successful prompt formats on development data while measuring both recipient decoding and correct reordered-donor availability. This would identify whether presentation changes preserve both capabilities rather than improve one at the other's expense.

## Appendix A: Experimental Details

### Common measured-experiment conventions

All six measured experiments used the released Hugging Face **Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct**, a 7B-class model with 7.616 billion recorded parameters, without weight updates or quantization. Inference used BF16 (16-bit bfloat16 numerical precision), scaled dot-product attention (SDPA), the native chat template, and complete untruncated prompts; each held-out test contained four files, four recipients, and exactly 600 permitted plus 600 forbidden requests.

Every file had one permitted recipient; recipients could repeat across files. Complete names and catalog-relative assignment vectors were disjoint across development and test. Linear classifiers used only one original post-block residual vector at the final nonpadding prompt token, before the model's terminal normalization; training-only coordinate scaling and an intercept preserve an affine decision function of that vector. All reported choices were frozen before testing.

Intervals below are 95% Wilson intervals unless marked **cluster**, meaning an interval obtained by repeatedly resampling whole permission assignments. Percentages are empirical finite-test rates, not confidence-bound success requirements. Tables show the test endpoints and controls bearing on validity; classwise breakdowns, development sweeps, checkpoint details, and exact seed schedules remain in the supplied results and code. The descriptions below identify each run by the part of the claim it measured.

### A.1 Requested-file readout

**Target:** ≥1,080/1,200 overall requested-file predictions and ≥90% among initial errors; a lower measured rate would be a shortfall for this configuration. **Data:** FourFileTransfer-Generated-v1, with 1,024 pilot, 4,096 fitting, 1,024 selection, 640 separate positive-control, and 1,200 test problems; recipient-rotation orbits allocated 128 permission vectors each to development and test. Fitting included 3,691 correct and 405 incorrect authorization runs.

**Procedure:** (1) Evaluate four naming presentations on development data and select the first qualifying error-bearing presentation. (2) Capture all block outputs at the final prompt token. (3) Fit standardized four-class affine probes, choose by selection accuracy and freeze. (4) Generate the test set, apply the saved decoder, and score original authorization subsets.

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Identity target and prompt | File-catalog position; independent opaque names |
| Selected state | Block 20, final prompt token |
| Decoder search | 28 blocks × weight decay {0, 0.0001, 0.01, 0.1}; selected 0.1 |
| Training | AdamW, learning rate 0.01, 80 epochs, batch 256 |
| Authorization | A = permitted, B = forbidden; next-token comparison |
| Compute | One H100 80GB; 270.9 s; inference batch 8; global seed 42, probe seed 5042 |

| Test condition | Correct / evaluated | Accuracy (%) | 95% interval (%) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| File decoder, all problems | 1,175 / 1,200 | 97.92 | 96.94–98.58 |
| File decoder, initial errors | 123 / 125 | 98.40 | 94.35–99.56 |
| File decoder, initially correct | 1,052 / 1,075 | 97.86 | 96.81–98.57 |
| Shuffled-label decoder, all | 258 / 1,200 | 21.50 | 19.27–23.91 |
| Constant catalog position | 300 / 1,200 | 25.00 | 22.63–27.53 |

The explicit-position positive control scored 118/128 on validation. Selected-block numerical extraction checks passed; batched/single extraction tolerance was missed at later, unselected blocks.

### A.2 Initial permitted-recipient readout

report:
# Decoding and repairing permission decisions in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Problem ID** | 515 |
| **Scenario** | Lack of adherence: Drift in long contexts, responses to knowledge conflict, incorrect tool use, bias |
| **Assessment Verdict** | +1 Likely feasible |
| **Likert Score** | +1 |
| **Confidence** | 0.82 |
| **Date** | 2026-10-05 |

## Bottom line
**+1 Likely feasible, confidence 0.82:** separate four-file/four-recipient tests of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct achieved 95.08% recipient decoding and nine-head repair of 93.01% of initial errors with no observed changes to initially correct decisions. The donor intervention changes the computation while preserving the permission facts, demonstrating selective repair rather than only a correlation between internal states and errors.

## 1. Introduction

> On 1,200 held-out file-transfer problems balanced between permitted and forbidden requests, with four files and four recipients, linear decoders of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct's final prompt-token residual state identify the requested file and its permitted recipient with at least 90% accuracy each, even among incorrect authorization decisions. Patching a fixed set of at most 12 attention heads from correct runs containing the same permission facts in reordered table rows corrects at least 30% of all initial errors while changing no more than 3% of correct decisions. Decoders, heads, and donor-selection rules are fixed on separate development data, with decoders trained on both correct and incorrect development runs; test names and permission assignments are unseen.

I read this as an existential claim that one development-fixed system must satisfy all six empirical thresholds on the same stipulated test set, with presentation, residual layer, identity-label mapping, and patch alignment left open.

1. Both identity decoders must reach 90% overall and separately among initial authorization errors: four criteria.
2. One fixed intervention using at most 12 heads must repair 30% of all initial errors and change at most 3% of initially correct decisions: two criteria.
3. Development/test separation, unseen names and assignments, and correct permission-equivalent donors must hold throughout.

Every part is needed; preserving recipient decodability while obtaining selective repair decides the claim. For this scenario, success would distinguish retained permission knowledge from a faulty decision and show that a targeted intervention can restore adherence.

## 2. What the literature establishes

A **binding** is the association between an entity and its attribute—for example, a file and its permitted recipient. The closest literature establishes useful mechanisms, but its numerical results depend strongly on task and readout.

| Closest work | Published result beside the claim's thresholds | Relevance and mismatch |
|---|---|---|
| Propositional probes | On Tulu-2-13B, proposition-set exact match is 97% on templates, 55% on paraphrases, and 26% on Spanish translations; under template prompt injection, probes retain 98% while prompting falls to 7%. Claim: each identity readout ≥90%. | Strong evidence that correct relations can survive misleading outputs. The complete decoder combines token-level linear probes with comparisons between entity and attribute token states to recover their association, rather than one final-token linear classifier. [lit_propositional_probes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19501) |
| Legible failures | Qwen2.5-7B Base wrong-trial binding accuracy is 27.6% (reported interval 23.6–34.5%) on eight choices. The paper's independent replication in its section 3.3 reports four-choice failure-conditioned accuracy of 47.4–79.9% across eight models, still below 90%. Qwen steering repairs 29% and preserves 79%, versus the claim's ≥30% repair and ≥97% preservation. | Closest published error-conditioned linear readout. Base versus Instruct, interference, and residual steering versus donor-head patching limit transfer. [lit_legible_failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11216) |
| Sparse Qwen head intervention | Eight candidate heads support a dynamic intervention that raises average Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct accuracy from 41.7% to 48.5%, or 61.3% when given the locations of erroneous predictions. Claim: one fixed set ≤12 heads with separate repair/disruption limits. | Direct support for sparse, model-specific correction, but aggregate accuracy does not establish either conditional intervention rate; heads are dynamically selected and ablated, not donor-patched. [lit_qwen_sparse_head_intervention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21214) |
| Fragile reasoning | On 60 selected perturbation-induced GSM8K failures, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct hidden-state patching repairs 0/60; residual steering recovers 7.2%. Claim: ≥30% repair. | Shows that a correct donor need not repair Qwen reasoning failures. Arithmetic generation and whole-state interventions differ from permission lookup and sparse-head replacement. [lit_fragile_reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01639) |

**The strongest published case for the claim** is the high template relation recovery, reinforced by the same-model sparse intervention gain. **The strongest published case against it** is the substantially sub-threshold failure-conditioned binding readout, together with Qwen's arithmetic patch failure. Their numbers are juxtaposed above: these findings disagree about transfer, not about whether internal information and emitted answers can differ. The positive case wins for this bounded permission task when weighed with the matched demonstrations below, while the negative case cautions against assuming that an arbitrary presentation will work.

## 3. What the literature leaves open

Requested-file recovery and permitted-recipient recovery require different operations: copying the queried identity versus retrieving its associated permission. We evaluated both from original final-prompt-token states, including error-conditioned results, because the published binding accuracies do not settle either requirement.

Sparse repair and preservation must be measured together, not inferred from an aggregate accuracy gain. Two experiments therefore applied the same frozen intervention to both initial outcome subsets; all decoding and intervention criteria together on one test set remain the next measurement.

## 4. What our experiments show

**Requested-file decoding.** With opaque identifiers, catalog-position labels, and a development-selected block-20 readout, accuracy was 1,175/1,200 = 97.92% (95% Wilson interval 96.94–98.58%, a confidence interval for a binomial proportion). The same frozen decoder's descriptive error subset scored 123/125 = 98.40% (94.35–99.56%), exceeding both requested-file thresholds. [experiment_sc1]

**Initial recipient decoding—shared-stem names, request before a reversed-column table, and 8,192 training examples.** The frozen linear readout recovered 849/1,200 = 70.75% (95% interval 67.85–73.51%, calculated by resampling permission assignments), against 90%. [experiment_sc2]

**Recipient decoding during errors—confusable names, an inactive history record, and a converged linear readout.** Accuracy was 197/290 = 67.93% over initial authorization errors (95% Wilson interval 62.35–73.04%), against 90%. [experiment_sc4]

**Higher-data recipient decoding.** An independent presentation and split, approximately 65.54 thousand training examples, and a converged block-20 linear decoder produced 1,141/1,200 = 95.08% (95% interval 93.86–96.27%, calculated by resampling permission assignments). Its descriptive initial-error subset reached 300/309 = 97.09% (Wilson interval 94.56–98.46%); this demonstrates both recipient targets, although the changed data, presentation, and optimization do not isolate a single fix for the earlier shortfalls. [experiment_sc102] [compute_6]

**Semantically aligned head patching.** Eleven development-fixed heads, patched at corresponding prompt-token positions from the first correct reordered donor, repaired 112/123 = 91.06% of all initial errors (95% Wilson interval 84.69–94.93%). Only 2/1,077 = 0.1857% of initially correct decisions changed (0.05094–0.6746%), comfortably satisfying both intervention limits. [experiment_sc5]

**Final-token head patching.** Nine fixed heads with a maximum-correct-margin donor rule repaired 213/229 = 93.01% of all errors (95% Wilson interval 88.95–95.65%). They changed 0/971 correct decisions (interval 0–0.3941%); donors unavailable for some errors remained in the denominator, and this was an active repair intervention, not a preservation-only no-op. [experiment_sc6]

See Appendix A for experimental details and for runs that produced no measurement.

## 4b. In the News (non-academic sources)

**Concordance company blog, date not supplied; trust tier (news), self-report:** “Single model. All results are on Qwen3-30B-A3B. Cross-model transfer is untested.” This contextualizes interest in reading and modifying rule-compliance representations, but neither supports nor undermines the named Qwen2.5 claim quantitatively. [web_rule_compliance_representations](https://www.concordance.co/blog/reading-writing-rule-compliance-representations)

## 5. Why the claim succeeds or fails

**The claim requires readable identities and selective repair to coexist on one presentation.** The intervention need not use the probe's predictions, so the two methods can be optimized separately before their joint evaluation.

**The permission-task demonstrations are the decisive evidence.** They establish working capabilities in the named model under the claim's conditions, whereas the unfavorable published binding and arithmetic results measure different retrieval demands and intervention sites. [lit_legible_failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11216) [lit_fragile_reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01639)

**The next technical step is adapting the successful recipient readout to a presentation that also supports donor repair.** That requires keeping the retrieved recipient aligned with a stable catalog label as names and assignments change, rather than memorizing literal identifiers.

## 6. Assessment

**+1 Likely feasible, confidence 0.82:** for the approximately three-month feasibility assessment, a relevant interpretability lab is likely to achieve all six criteria with one frozen configuration. Confidence is limited because each experiment used one fixed set of random seeds; the reported intervals do not estimate variability across new development-data partitions.

**A development-frozen six-criterion pass would move the score to +2 Feasible.** Conversely, replicated matched results in which adequate recipient decoding consistently accompanies inadequate repair or excessive disruption—or successful repair consistently leaves decoding below its threshold—would move the assessment toward balance or likely infeasibility.

### Why not the neighbouring scores

**+2 Feasible would treat a demonstrated readout obstacle as routine:** the converged recipient decoder's substantial shortfall shows that this step is sensitive to implementation. **0 Evenly balanced would discount the diversity of successful repair:** two donor-selection rules and token scopes worked, so the positive case does not depend on one head-selection recipe.

## 7. Limitations and further directions

The error-subset successes for both decoders were descriptive analyses rather than separate primary hypotheses, reducing their confirmatory strength without changing the observed finite-test counts. Synthetic identifier tasks and immediate binary decisions support the claim's allowed setup, not a broader conclusion about long-workflow adherence. Ground-truth-assisted donor qualification is permitted here, but does not establish a deployable authorization safeguard.

**Further directions**

- Train both decoders and select the head intervention on one development distribution, then freeze everything before a new balanced 1,200-problem evaluation. A six-criterion pass would establish a complete working instance.
- Repeat that evaluation with independently held-out assignment pools and name seeds. Stable margins would strengthen confidence; systematic incompatibility would lower the score.
- Compare the successful prompt formats on development data while measuring both recipient decoding and correct reordered-donor availability. This would identify whether presentation changes preserve both capabilities rather than improve one at the other's expense.

## Appendix A: Experimental Details

### Common measured-experiment conventions

All six measured experiments used the released Hugging Face **Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct**, a 7B-class model with 7.616 billion recorded parameters, without weight updates or quantization. Inference used BF16 (16-bit bfloat16 numerical precision), scaled dot-product attention (SDPA), the native chat template, and complete untruncated prompts; each held-out test contained four files, four recipients, and exactly 600 permitted plus 600 forbidden requests. [experiment_sc1] [experiment_sc102]

Every file had one permitted recipient; recipients could repeat across files. Complete names and catalog-relative assignment vectors were disjoint across development/test. Linear classifiers used only one original post-block residual vector at the final nonpadding prompt token, before the model's terminal normalization; training-only coordinate scaling and an intercept preserve an affine decision function of that vector. All reported choices were frozen before testing. [experiment_sc2] [experiment_sc4]

Intervals below are 95% Wilson intervals unless marked **cluster**, meaning an interval obtained by repeatedly resampling whole permission assignments. Percentages are empirical finite-test rates, not confidence-bound success requirements. Tables show the test endpoints and controls bearing on validity; classwise breakdowns, development sweeps, checkpoint details, and exact seed schedules remain in the supplied results and code.

### A.1 Requested-file readout

**Target:** ≥1,080/1,200 overall requested-file predictions and ≥90% among initial errors; a lower measured rate would be a shortfall for this configuration. **Data:** FourFileTransfer-Generated-v1, with 1,024 pilot, 4,096 fitting, 1,024 selection, 640 separate positive-control, and 1,200 test problems; recipient-rotation orbits allocated 128 permission vectors each to development and test. Fitting included 3,691 correct and 405 incorrect authorization runs. [experiment_sc1]

**Procedure:** (1) Evaluate four naming presentations on development data and select the first qualifying error-bearing presentation. (2) Capture all block outputs at the final prompt token. (3) Fit standardized four-class affine probes, choose by selection accuracy and freeze. (4) Generate the test set, apply the saved decoder, and score original authorization subsets.

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Identity target and prompt | File-catalog position; independent opaque names |
| Selected state | Block 20, final prompt token |
| Decoder search | 28 blocks × weight decay {0, 0.0001, 0.01, 0.1}; selected 0.1 |
| Training | AdamW, learning rate 0.01, 80 epochs, batch 256 |
| Authorization | A = permitted, B = forbidden; next-token comparison |
| Compute | One H100 80GB; 270.9 s; inference batch 8; global seed 42, probe seed 5042 |

| Test condition | Correct / evaluated | Accuracy (%) | 95% interval (%) |

report:
# Decoding and repairing permission decisions in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Problem ID** | 515 |
| **Scenario** | Lack of adherence: Drift in long contexts, responses to knowledge conflict, incorrect tool use, bias |
| **Assessment Verdict** | +1 Likely feasible |
| **Likert Score** | +1 |
| **Confidence** | 0.82 |
| **Date** | 2026-10-05 |

## Bottom line
**+1 Likely feasible, confidence 0.82:** in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct permission tests, fact-equivalent row reorderings supplied correct donors for sparse head replacement that repaired errors while preserving correct decisions. Successful linear identity readouts make this a task-presentation adaptation problem rather than a search for an entirely new internal recovery mechanism.

## 1. Introduction

> On 1,200 held-out file-transfer problems balanced between permitted and forbidden requests, with four files and four recipients, linear decoders of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct's final prompt-token residual state identify the requested file and its permitted recipient with at least 90% accuracy each, even among incorrect authorization decisions. Patching a fixed set of at most 12 attention heads from correct runs containing the same permission facts in reordered table rows corrects at least 30% of all initial errors while changing no more than 3% of correct decisions. Decoders, heads, and donor-selection rules are fixed on separate development data, with decoders trained on both correct and incorrect development runs; test names and permission assignments are unseen.

I read this as an existential claim that one development-fixed system must satisfy all six empirical thresholds on the same stipulated test set, with presentation, residual layer, identity-label mapping, and patch alignment left open.

1. Both identity decoders must reach 90% overall and separately among initial authorization errors: four criteria.
2. One fixed intervention using at most 12 heads must repair 30% of all initial errors and change at most 3% of initially correct decisions: two criteria.
3. Development/test separation, unseen names and assignments, and correct permission-equivalent donors must hold throughout.

Every part is needed; preserving recipient decodability while obtaining selective repair decides the claim. For this scenario, success would distinguish retained permission knowledge from a faulty decision and show that a targeted intervention can restore adherence.

## 2. What the literature establishes

A **binding** is the association between an entity and its attribute—for example, a file and its permitted recipient. The closest literature establishes useful mechanisms, but its numerical results depend strongly on task and readout.

| Closest work | Published result beside the claim's thresholds | Relevance and mismatch |
|---|---|---|
| Propositional probes | On Tulu-2-13B, accuracy for recovering all stated relations correctly is 97% on templates, 55% on paraphrases, and 26% on Spanish translations; under template prompt injection, probes retain 98% while prompting falls to 7%. Claim: each identity readout ≥90%. | Strong evidence that correct relations can survive misleading outputs. The complete decoder combines token-level linear probes with comparisons between entity and attribute token states to recover their association, rather than one final-token linear classifier. [lit_propositional_probes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19501) |
| Legible failures | Qwen2.5-7B Base wrong-trial binding accuracy is 27.6% (reported interval 23.6–34.5%) on eight choices. The full text's independent replication in section 3.3 reports four-choice failure-conditioned accuracy of 47.4–79.9% across eight models, still below 90%. Qwen steering—adding a direction vector to the residual state—repairs 29% and preserves 79%, versus the claim's ≥30% repair and ≥97% preservation. | Closest published error-conditioned linear readout. Base versus Instruct, interference, and residual steering versus donor-head patching limit transfer. The four-choice percentages are converted from the paper's reported proportions. [lit_legible_failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11216) [compute_7] |
| Sparse Qwen head intervention | Eight candidate heads support a dynamic intervention that raises average Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct accuracy from 41.7% to 48.5%, or 61.3% when given the locations of erroneous predictions. Claim: one fixed set ≤12 heads with separate repair/disruption limits. | Direct support for sparse, model-specific correction, but aggregate accuracy does not establish either conditional intervention rate; heads are dynamically selected and ablated, not donor-patched. [lit_qwen_sparse_head_intervention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21214) |
| Fragile reasoning | On 60 selected perturbation-induced GSM8K failures, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct hidden-state patching repairs 0/60; residual steering recovers 7.2%. Claim: ≥30% repair. | Shows that a correct donor need not repair Qwen reasoning failures. Arithmetic generation and whole-state interventions differ from permission lookup and sparse-head replacement. [lit_fragile_reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01639) |

**The strongest published case for the claim** is the high template relation recovery, reinforced by the same-model sparse intervention gain. **The strongest published case against it** is the substantially sub-threshold failure-conditioned binding readout, together with Qwen's arithmetic patch failure. Their numbers are juxtaposed above: these findings disagree about transfer, not about whether internal information and emitted answers can differ. The positive case wins for this bounded permission task when weighed with the matched demonstrations below, while the negative case cautions against assuming that an arbitrary presentation will work.

## 3. What the literature leaves open

Requested-file recovery and permitted-recipient recovery require different operations: copying the queried identity versus retrieving its associated permission. We evaluated both from original final-prompt-token states, including error-conditioned results, because the published binding accuracies do not settle either requirement.

Sparse repair and preservation must be measured together, not inferred from an aggregate accuracy gain. Two experiments therefore applied the same frozen intervention to both initial outcome subsets; all decoding and intervention criteria together on one test set remain the next measurement.

## 4. What our experiments show

**Requested-file decoding.** With opaque identifiers, catalog-position labels, and a development-selected block-20 readout, accuracy was 1,175/1,200 = 97.92% (95% Wilson interval 96.94–98.58%, a confidence interval for a binomial proportion). The same frozen decoder's descriptive error subset scored 123/125 = 98.40% (94.35–99.56%), exceeding both requested-file thresholds. [experiment_sc1]

**Initial recipient decoding—shared-stem names, request before a reversed-column table, and 8,192 training examples.** The frozen linear readout recovered 849/1,200 = 70.75% (95% interval 67.85–73.51%, calculated by resampling permission assignments), against 90%. [experiment_sc2]

**Recipient decoding during errors—confusable names, an inactive history record, and a converged linear readout.** Accuracy was 197/290 = 67.93% over initial authorization errors (95% Wilson interval 62.35–73.04%), against 90%. [experiment_sc4]

**Higher-data recipient decoding.** An independent presentation and split, approximately 65.54 thousand training examples, and a converged block-20 linear decoder produced 1,141/1,200 = 95.08% (95% interval 93.86–96.27%, calculated by resampling permission assignments). Its descriptive initial-error subset reached 300/309 = 97.09% (Wilson interval 94.56–98.46%); this demonstrates both recipient targets, although the changed data, presentation, and optimization do not isolate a single fix for the earlier shortfalls. [experiment_sc102] [compute_6]

**Semantically aligned head patching.** Eleven development-fixed heads, patched at corresponding prompt-token positions from the first correct reordered donor, repaired 112/123 = 91.06% of all initial errors (95% Wilson interval 84.69–94.93%). Only 2/1,077 = 0.1857% of initially correct decisions changed (0.05094–0.6746%), comfortably satisfying both intervention limits. [experiment_sc5]

**Final-token head patching.** Nine fixed heads with a maximum-correct-margin donor rule repaired 213/229 = 93.01% of all errors (95% Wilson interval 88.95–95.65%). They changed 0/971 correct decisions (interval 0–0.3941%); donors unavailable for some errors remained in the denominator, and this was an active repair intervention, not a preservation-only no-op. [experiment_sc6]

See Appendix A for experimental details and for runs that produced no measurement.

## 4b. In the News (non-academic sources)

**Concordance company blog, date not supplied; trust tier (news), self-report:** “Single model. All results are on Qwen3-30B-A3B. Cross-model transfer is untested.” This contextualizes interest in reading and modifying rule-compliance representations, but neither supports nor undermines the named Qwen2.5 claim quantitatively. [web_rule_compliance_representations](https://www.concordance.co/blog/reading-writing-rule-compliance-representations)

## 5. Why the claim succeeds or fails

**The claim requires readable identities and selective repair to coexist on one presentation.** The intervention need not use the probe's predictions, so the two methods can be optimized separately before their joint evaluation.

**The permission-task demonstrations are the decisive evidence.** They establish working capabilities in the named model under the claim's conditions, whereas the unfavorable published binding and arithmetic results measure different retrieval demands and intervention sites. [lit_legible_failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11216) [lit_fragile_reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01639)

**The next technical step is adapting the successful recipient readout to a presentation that also supports donor repair.** That requires keeping the retrieved recipient aligned with a stable catalog label as names and assignments change, rather than memorizing literal identifiers.

## 6. Assessment

**+1 Likely feasible, confidence 0.82:** for the approximately three-month feasibility assessment, a relevant interpretability lab is likely to achieve all six criteria with one frozen configuration. Confidence is limited because each experiment used one fixed set of random seeds; the reported intervals do not estimate variability across new development-data partitions.

**A development-frozen six-criterion pass would move the score to +2 Feasible.** Conversely, replicated matched results in which adequate recipient decoding consistently accompanies inadequate repair or excessive disruption—or successful repair consistently leaves decoding below its threshold—would move the assessment toward balance or likely infeasibility.

### Why not the neighbouring scores

**+2 Feasible would treat a demonstrated readout obstacle as routine:** the converged recipient decoder's substantial shortfall shows that this step is sensitive to implementation. **0 Evenly balanced would discount the diversity of successful repair:** two donor-selection rules and token scopes worked, so the positive case does not depend on one head-selection recipe.

## 7. Limitations and further directions

The error-subset successes for both decoders were descriptive analyses rather than separate primary hypotheses, reducing their confirmatory strength without changing the observed finite-test counts. Synthetic identifier tasks and immediate binary decisions support the claim's allowed setup, not a broader conclusion about long-workflow adherence. Ground-truth-assisted donor qualification is permitted here, but does not establish a deployable authorization safeguard.

**Further directions**

- Train both decoders and select the head intervention on one development distribution, then freeze everything before a new balanced 1,200-problem evaluation. A six-criterion pass would establish a complete working instance.
- Repeat that evaluation with independently held-out assignment pools and name seeds. Stable margins would strengthen confidence; systematic incompatibility would lower the score.
- Compare the successful prompt formats on development data while measuring both recipient decoding and correct reordered-donor availability. This would identify whether presentation changes preserve both capabilities rather than improve one at the other's expense.

## Appendix A: Experimental Details

### Common measured-experiment conventions

All six measured experiments used the released Hugging Face **Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct**, a 7B-class model with 7.616 billion recorded parameters, without weight updates or quantization. Inference used BF16 (16-bit bfloat16 numerical precision), scaled dot-product attention (SDPA), the native chat template, and complete untruncated prompts; each held-out test contained four files, four recipients, and exactly 600 permitted plus 600 forbidden requests. [experiment_sc1] [experiment_sc102]

Every file had one permitted recipient; recipients could repeat across files. Complete names and catalog-relative assignment vectors were disjoint across development/test. Linear classifiers used only one original post-block residual vector at the final nonpadding prompt token, before the model's terminal normalization; training-only coordinate scaling and an intercept preserve an affine decision function of that vector. All reported choices were frozen before testing. [experiment_sc2] [experiment_sc4]

Intervals below are 95% Wilson intervals unless marked **cluster**, meaning an interval obtained by repeatedly resampling whole permission assignments. Percentages are empirical finite-test rates, not confidence-bound success requirements. Tables show the test endpoints and controls bearing on validity; classwise breakdowns, development sweeps, checkpoint details, and exact seed schedules remain in the supplied results and code.

### A.1 Requested-file readout

**Target:** ≥1,080/1,200 overall requested-file predictions and ≥90% among initial errors; a lower measured rate would be a shortfall for this configuration. **Data:** FourFileTransfer-Generated-v1, with 1,024 pilot, 4,096 fitting, 1,024 selection, 640 separate positive-control, and 1,200 test problems; recipient-rotation orbits allocated 128 permission vectors each to development and test. Fitting included 3,691 correct and 405 incorrect authorization runs. [experiment_sc1]

**Procedure:** (1) Evaluate four naming presentations on development data and select the first qualifying error-bearing presentation. (2) Capture all block outputs at the final prompt token. (3) Fit standardized four-class affine probes, choose by selection accuracy and freeze. (4) Generate the test set, apply the saved decoder, and score original authorization subsets.

| Compute | One H100 80GB; 270.9 s; inference batch 8; global seed 42, probe seed 5042 |

Fitting included 4,874 correct and 3,318 incorrect authorization runs. [experiment_sc2]

(3) Fit standardized affine softmax probes with L2 regularization, a squared-weight penalty, and select on development recipient accuracy. (4) Freeze the decoder and evaluate all untouched test problems, including descriptive error subsets.

### A.4 Independent higher-data recipient readout

**Target:** ≥1,080/1,200 overall recipient predictions; the error subset was reported descriptively. **Data:** the independent higher-data version of FourFilePermissionBinding-v1, with approximately 65.54 thousand fitting, 8,192 selection, and 1,200 new test problems; a fresh 160/32/64 assignment partition and collision-checked names. Fitting included approximately 47.7 thousand correct and 17.83 thousand incorrect authorization decisions. [experiment_sc102] [compute_6]

### A.5 Eleven-head, semantically aligned donor intervention

**Target:** ≥30% repair over all initial errors and ≤3% changes over all initially correct decisions. **Data:** FT4x4-RowRepair-v1, with four 256-problem pilots, 1,024 discovery, 512 intervention-validation, and 1,200 test problems; 128 development and 128 held-out assignment vectors. [experiment_sc5]

**Procedure:** (1) Calibrate presentation and enumerate row permutations. (2) Rank heads using gradient-times-donor-difference attribution, then exact sparse tests and bounded greedy selection. (3) Select one head set and token scope on separate validation data and freeze. (4) Apply the same patch, self-patch control, and random-head control to all test problems; retain donor-unavailable errors.

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Prompt | Conventional File / Permitted recipient table; ordinary identifiers |
| Donor selection | First correct of 23 nonidentity relative permutations; same request and facts |
| Patch | Query-head outputs before output projection; matching prompt-token positions, with unmatched boundaries untouched |
| Selected heads, zero-based (layer, head) | (12,24), (15,3), (17,22), (18,4), (18,13), (18,15), (18,18), (18,21), (19,23), (19,24), (20,3) |
| Readout/numerics | A/B authorization; BF16 backbone, FP32 accumulation for ordinary A/B output weights; fixed batch shapes |
| Unavailable donor handling | No patch; keep the case in its original denominator |
| Compute | One H100 80GB; 2,321 s; inference batch 16, gradient batch 2; global seed 42, partition 421, discovery 423, validation 424, test 425 |

### A.6 Nine-head, final-token donor intervention

**Target:** the same coupled repair/preservation criteria as A.5. **Data:** SyntheticFileTransfer4x4-v1, with eight 128-problem pilots, 384 discovery, 384 search, 768 validation, and 1,200 test problems; disjoint assignment pools contained 32/64/64/32/64 vectors respectively. [experiment_sc6]

**Procedure:** (1) Calibrate identifier similarity on development data. (2) Rank all heads, shortlist candidates, and perform exact greedy subset searches. (3) Validate candidate sets and freeze the head set, final-token scope, and donor rule. (4) Evaluate original decisions, qualify and recapture donors, patch every eligible test case, and retain all original denominators.

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Prompt | Conventional table followed by request; 16-character confusable identifiers differing at the end |
| Donor selection | Maximum correct signed A/B margin among 23 reordered views; lexicographic ties; capture-time requalification |
| Patch | Query-head outputs before output projection, final prompt token only |
| Selected heads, zero-based (layer, head) | (18,4), (18,13), (18,15), (18,18), (19,23), (19,24), (20,1), (20,3), (26,26) |
| Authorization | A = permitted, B = forbidden; ties A |
| Unavailable donor handling | No patch; all errors and initially correct decisions retained |
| Compute | One H100 80GB; 926.7 s; inference batch 16, gradient batch 2; seed 42 |

| Intervention | Errors repaired / all errors | Repair % [95% interval] | Correct decisions changed / all initially correct | Change % [95% interval] |

Sampled self-patches reproduced logits exactly; the custom-versus-standard forward comparison missed a strict logit tolerance by 0.125, although decisions agreed. | What it tested | Why no measurement is used | Record |

## Appendix C: Claim Card

| Element | Locked reading |
|---|---|
| System under test | Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct making permission-based file-transfer authorization decisions; linear residual-state decoders and inference-time attention-head patches |
| Claimed property | Recovery of requested-file and permitted-recipient identities despite incorrect decisions, plus selective correction of those decisions |
| Conditions | Four files/four recipients; 1,200 held-out problems, balanced 600 permitted/600 forbidden; unseen test names and permission assignments; original final prompt-token states; development-frozen decoders trained on both correct and incorrect runs; one fixed set of at most 12 heads; fixed donor rules; correct donors with the same permission facts in reordered rows |
| Quantifier | Existential: one system satisfying every criterion is sufficient |
| Success threshold | File and recipient accuracies each ≥90% overall and separately among all initial errors; repair ≥30% of all initial errors; authorization-decision changes ≤3% of all initially correct decisions; all six together |
| Comparator | Decoder ground truth; for intervention effects, the same problems' original unpatched authorization decisions |
| Fixed scoring assumptions | Unambiguous task ground truth; prespecified identity-label mapping for unseen names; wording-independent authorization extraction; nonempty initial correct/error subsets |
| Fixed intervention assumptions | Accessible residual/head activations and alignable donors; comparable patched/unpatched inference; prespecified donor-correctness and unavailable-donor handling without removing errors |
| Fixed separation assumptions | Enforceable novelty and development/test separation; no test refitting, head reselection, or revision of donor rules |
| Choices left open | Generator and prompt format, development-data size, residual layer/normalization, affine decoder fitting, head identities, patch components/positions/alignment, donor search and request matching, response format, checkpoint revision, precision, and seeds |

The empirical thresholds and conditions are those of the supplied claim; the assessment does not require causal use of the decoded identities, production deployment, or generalization beyond the stated test setup. [claim_verbatim]

"### Target and primary endpoint

Run `Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct`, revision `a09a354`, without weight updates or quantization.

The sole primary endpoint is the frozen linear decoder’s requested-file accuracy on **all 1,200 test problems**:

- Four files and four recipients per problem.
- Exactly 600 permitted and 600 forbidden requests.
- Exactly 300 requests for each of four catalog positions; within each position, 150 permitted and 150 forbidden.
- Success: at least **1,080 correct predictions**.
- Failure on this protocol: fewer than 1,080 correct predictions, provided the pipeline checks and required development-data conditions passed.

Authorization correctness is recorded to establish that decoder training includes correct and incorrect runs. Error-conditioned requested-file accuracy can be reported descriptively, but is not a second primary hypothesis.

### 1. Construct an auditable development/test split

Create the synthetic dataset `FourFileTransfer-Generated-v1`; no external dataset is required.

Each problem has ordered file and recipient catalogs, `F[0:4]` and `R[0:4]`. Every file has exactly one permitted recipient. Represent its permission assignment by:

`m = (m[0], m[1], m[2], m[3])`, where each entry is in `{0,1,2,3}`.

Allow multiple files to share a recipient. All four recipients remain explicitly listed.

Partition the 256 possible mapping vectors into 64 orbits under global cyclic relabeling of recipients. With seed 42, shuffle the orbits and allocate 32 complete orbits to development and 32 to test: **128 mapping vectors in each pool, with no intersection**. Using complete orbits balances recipient indices within each pool.

Use new full file and recipient identifiers in every problem. Assign names to catalog positions randomly, independently of suffix order and labels. Maintain a registry of all development identifiers and reject any test identifier collision.

Each permission-table row contains a file name and its permitted recipient name. Randomize table-row order independently of catalog order. A permitted request names `F[j]` and `R[m[j]]`; a forbidden request names `F[j]` and one of the other three recipients.

The decoding label is `j`, the requested file’s position in the ordered file catalog. It is computed by the generator and is never added to the primary request text.

# Decoding and repairing file-transfer authorization in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Problem ID** | 515 |
| **Scenario** | Lack of adherence: Drift in long contexts, responses to knowledge conflict, incorrect tool use, bias |
| **Assessment Verdict** | +1 Likely feasible |
| **Likert Score** | +1 |
| **Confidence** | 0.78 |
| **Date** | 2026-10-05 |

## Bottom line

Correct permission information can remain accessible despite a wrong authorization decision: a frozen recipient decoder exceeds 90% even on errors, while a working nine-head intervention exceeds the repair target without changing any initially correct decisions. The assessment is **+1 Likely feasible**, score **+1**, confidence **0.78**: the remaining hurdle is achieving the decoder and intervention results together under one frozen presentation and test distribution, rather than combining successes from different setups. [experiment_sc102] [experiment_sc6]

## 1. Introduction

> On 1,200 held-out file-transfer problems balanced between permitted and forbidden requests, with four files and four recipients, linear decoders of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct's final prompt-token residual state identify the requested file and its permitted recipient with at least 90% accuracy each, even among incorrect authorization decisions. Patching a fixed set of at most 12 attention heads from correct runs containing the same permission facts in reordered table rows corrects at least 30% of all initial errors while changing no more than 3% of correct decisions. Decoders, heads, and donor-selection rules are fixed on separate development data, with decoders trained on both correct and incorrect development runs; test names and permission assignments are unseen.

I read this as an existential claim that one development-fixed configuration of the named model meets all six accuracy and intervention-rate criteria on the same held-out set, with identity labels defined consistently for unseen names and correct donors verified by a prespecified procedure.

1. Both identities must be decoded at least 90% accurately overall and separately among all initial authorization errors.
2. One fixed set of at most 12 heads must repair at least 30% of all initial errors while changing at most 3% of initially correct decisions.
3. Development/test separation, unseen names and assignments, and frozen selection rules must hold throughout.

Every part is required; their joint compatibility, particularly recipient decoding on the error distribution used for patching, decides the claim. This would distinguish inaccessible permission information from information the model represents but fails to use, enabling targeted adherence interventions.

## 2. What the literature establishes

The closest work concerns **binding**, the internal association between an entity and its attribute—in this case, a file and its permitted recipient.

| Prior work | Published result beside the claim's threshold | Relevance and boundary |
|---|---|---|
| *Legible failures* | Qwen2.5-7B **Base**: failure-conditioned linear binding accuracy 27.6%, seed range 23.6–34.5%, versus the claim's 90%. In a separate steering setting: 29% repair and 79% preservation, versus required 30% repair and at least 97% preservation. | Direct evidence that prompt-supplied bindings can survive wrong answers, but neither its model variant nor residual-direction intervention matches the claim. [web_legible_failures_error_decoding_and_steering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11216) |
| *How do Language Models Bind Entities in Context?* | On two-binding tests, control accuracy exceeds 99%; separate entity or attribute interventions reduce original-association accuracy below 3%; simultaneous interventions restore it above 97%. | Establishes manipulable binding representations in LLaMA/Pythia. The restoration reverses an artificial intervention, not natural authorization errors, and does not establish sparse-head repair. [web_binding_id_representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.17191) |
| *Mixing Mechanisms* | A model combining positional, lexical and direct-pointer retrieval achieves 0.95 Jensen–Shannon similarity, a measure of agreement between probability distributions. Experiments include Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. | Supports causal accessibility at the final token, but 0.95 distribution similarity is not 95% identity-decoding accuracy. Different retrieval signals make fact-equivalent row orders potentially different activation donors. [web_mixing_mechanisms_qwen_binding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.06182) |

**The strongest published case for the claim** is the instruction-tuned OLMo binding result in *Legible failures*: 38% repair with 97% preservation already meets the claimed intervention-rate trade-off, albeit with residual steering rather than donor-head replacement. **The strongest published case against it** is the same paper's Qwen Base result above; even its four-binding replication across other models reaches only 47.4–79.9% failure-conditioned decoding. These results establish an actionable mechanism, not the conjunction of thresholds; the negative case survives as a warning about model, presentation and intervention-site dependence, rather than a bound on the four-file Instruct task. [web_legible_failures_error_decoding_and_steering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11216)

## 3. What the literature leaves open

The literature does not settle identity decoding with unseen names and assignments on this authorization task. Frozen linear-decoder experiments therefore tested requested-file decoding, overall recipient decoding, and recipient decoding among initial errors; a higher-data recipient experiment tested whether a stronger readout could close the observed shortfall.

Nor does residual steering settle the fixed-head donor intervention. Two experiments tested active head-output replacement from correct row-reordered donors, scoring repair and preservation together; none measured both decoders and patching in one configuration.

## 4. What our experiments show

Intervals below are supplementary 95% Wilson intervals; the claim itself specifies finite-set point thresholds.

**Requested-file decoding cleared both file accuracy bounds in one distribution.** A block-20 decoder trained on correct and incorrect development runs achieved 1,175/1,200, or 97.92% accuracy (96.94–98.58%), against 90%. Its supplementary initial-error result was 123/125, or 98.40% (94.35–99.56%); recipient decoding and patching were not tested. [experiment_sc1]

**The smaller overall-recipient experiment fell substantially short.** With shared-stem identifiers, the request before a reversed-column table, and 8,192 training problems, the selected block-20 decoder achieved 849/1,200, or 70.75% (68.11–73.25%), against 90%. Above-control performance shows a learned but insufficient readout, not a nonfunctioning method. [experiment_sc2]

**Recipient decoding on errors also failed in a history-containing presentation.** A converged decoder trained on 4,096 development problems achieved 197/290, or 67.93% (62.35–73.04%), among all initial errors, against 90%. This is direct negative evidence for that admissible presentation, including confusable names and explicitly nonauthoritative routing history. [experiment_sc4]

**Eleven-head patching met both intervention bounds.** Replacing outputs at semantically aligned tokens repaired 112/123 errors, or 91.06% (84.69–94.93%), against 30%, while changing 2/1,077 correct decisions, or 0.1857% (0.05094–0.6746%), against 3%. Two errors without qualifying donors remained in the denominator; self-patching and random-head controls supported a selective intervention effect. [experiment_sc5]

**Nine-head final-token patching independently met the coupled bounds.** The development-fixed intervention repaired 213/229 errors, or 93.01% (88.95–95.65%), and changed 0/971 correct decisions, or 0% (upper interval bound 0.3941%). It used a different frozen donor-ranking rule and presentation, so it demonstrates another working intervention instance, not decoder compatibility. [experiment_sc6]

**The higher-data recipient experiment cleared the recipient bounds.** With 65,536 training problems, independent shared-stem names and catalog-slot labels, the frozen block-20 decoder achieved 1,141/1,200, or 95.08% (93.71–96.17%). Its supplementary initial-error result was 300/309, or 97.09% (94.56–98.46%), against 90%; the changed presentation and training procedure prevent attributing the improvement over the smaller experiment solely to dataset size. [experiment_sc102]

See Appendix A for experimental details and for runs that produced no measurement.

## 4b. In the News (non-academic sources)

The news and podcast channel found no relevant items.

## 5. Why the claim succeeds or fails

**The claim can be true if authorization errors leave the file–recipient association readable and reordered donors supply a better retrieval computation.** Binding interventions establish that associations are causally manipulable, while Qwen's mixed retrieval mechanisms explain why equivalent facts can produce different internal states. The claim allows choosing the residual layer, token alignment and donor procedure on development data; it does not require label-free donor verification or universal success across prompt formats. [web_binding_id_representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.17191) [web_mixing_mechanisms_qwen_binding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.06182)

**The strongest evidence is now on the named authorization task, not merely analogous binding tasks.** Recipient decoding reached 95.08% overall and 97.09% on errors, while final-token sparse patching reached 93.01% repair with no observed correct-decision changes. Those working instances outweigh the much lower published Qwen Base results for these components, but they use different presentations and do not establish the full conjunction. [experiment_sc102] [experiment_sc6]

**Joint generalization remains the key driver, and the evidence shows a concrete route toward it.** The converged history-presentation decoder's 67.93% error accuracy is a real shortfall, not an optimization failure that can simply be dismissed. Within the higher-data presentation, a fixed layer and penalty yielded development-selection accuracies of 89.72%, 93.31% and 95.13% as training grew from 8,192 to 32,768 to 65,536 problems: generalization improved within one controlled readout family. This supports training a sufficiently strong decoder, but does not demonstrate that it retains those accuracies on the initial-error distribution where the sparse patch succeeds. [experiment_sc4] [compute_2]

## 6. Assessment

**The evidence favors +1 Likely feasible, score +1, confidence 0.78, within about three months for a relevant mechanistic-interpretability lab.** The estimate rests on component demonstrations with substantial threshold margins and a measured decoder learning curve, rather than on presumed resources or an unspecified future breakthrough. Confidence is below a demonstrated-feasibility judgment because the successful readouts and interventions were selected for different presentations, and the literature shows strong dependence on retrieval setting. [experiment_sc102] [web_legible_failures_error_decoding_and_steering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11216)

**A single joint held-out demonstration would move the score up; repeated joint shortfalls would move it down.** An independently frozen configuration satisfying all four decoder bounds and both patching bounds would justify +2 Feasible. Conversely, if the high-data decoder falls below 90% on the sparse-patching error distribution, or the corresponding fixed patch cannot maintain at least 30% repair with at most 3% changes, repeated well-functioning attempts would undermine the compatibility argument and lower the score. These tests directly connect the existing isolated successes. [experiment_sc102] [experiment_sc6]

### Why not the neighbouring scores

**+2 Feasible would overstate demonstrated compatibility, while 0 Evenly balanced would underweight the working components.** The high-data catalog readout has not been shown to coexist with the nine-head patch on the same presentation and original errors, so transfer between those specific configurations remains consequential. Nevertheless, 95.08% overall recipient decoding, 97.09% error-conditioned decoding, and 93.01% repair with zero observed disruption are positive measurements beyond the required bounds, not merely reasons the claim cannot be ruled out. [experiment_sc102] [experiment_sc6]

## 7. Limitations and further directions

The sampled-task intervals do not measure variation across independently trained decoders or head selections. These synthetic, single-token authorization tasks also do not establish persistent adherence in long workflows; donor checking uses task ground truth, which is allowed here but does not demonstrate autonomous deployment. [experiment_sc102] [experiment_sc5]

**Further directions**

- Train both identity decoders on one patch-compatible development distribution, freeze every choice, and evaluate all six criteria on the same 1,200 held-out problems. Passing would establish the joint instance; failing would locate the remaining incompatibility.
- Repeat the recipient learning curve under an unchanged prompt, label mapping and permission split, including all initial errors. This would distinguish sample-size gains from presentation changes and determine whether the decoder shortfalls have a demonstrated remedy.
- Repeat the joint configuration with independent development/test draws and fixed donor budgets. Stable margins would strengthen confidence; unstable conditional decoding or preservation would lower it.

## Appendix A: Experimental Details

All measured experiments used the Hugging Face **Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct** checkpoint, revision `a09a35458c702b33eeacc393d103063234e8bc28`: 7.616 billion parameters, frozen BF16 weights, native chat template, SDPA attention, and no quantization or generated reasoning. Every test contained four files, four recipients and exactly 600 permitted plus 600 forbidden requests; test names and canonical permission assignments were disjoint from development. Decoder inputs were one original, unnormalized post-block residual vector at the final actual prompt token; training-only coordinate standardization and affine classifiers preserved linear readouts. Model weights were never updated. [experiment_sc1] [experiment_sc102]

Percentages and intervals below retain the records' endpoint definitions. Wilson intervals are 95% unless stated; reported cluster bootstraps address repeated permission assignments. Uncertainty not supplied for a control is marked “not reported,” rather than inferred.

### A.1 Requested-file decoder

**Target:** at least 90% requested-file accuracy overall and on initial errors; lower measured accuracy would fail the relevant bound. **Model:** common Qwen checkpoint above. **Data:** locally generated FourFileTransfer-Generated-v1; 4,096 fitting, 1,024 validation, four pilots of 256, and a separate 512/128 disclosed-label control. Complete cyclic recipient-relabeling orbits divided permission vectors into 128 development and 128 test assignments.

**Procedure:** (1) Select the first prespecified pilot with a nontrivial error signal; independent opaque names were chosen. (2) Extract all block states and fit every layer/regularization candidate using both correctness groups. (3) Select on validation, freeze, generate the test set and score one selected decoder plus controls. Training included 3,691 correct and 405 incorrect authorization runs.

| Setting | Actual value |
|---|---|
| Identity labels / decision readout | File catalog position / A permitted, B forbidden |
| Selected residual block / weight decay | 20 / 0.1 |
| Training | AdamW; learning rate 0.01; 80 epochs; probe batches 256 |
| Candidate search | 28 blocks × four weight decays |
| Compute | One H100 80GB; 270.9 s; seed 42; inference batches 8 |

| Condition | Correct / evaluated | Accuracy (%) | 95% Wilson interval (%) |

| Disclosed-label control, validation | 118/128 | 92.19 | Not reported in the control record |

The selected block passed the extraction comparison; stricter batched/single-example tolerances failed at later, unselected blocks. [experiment_sc1]

### A.2 Smaller overall-recipient decoder

**Target:** at least 1,080 recipient predictions correct out of 1,200. **Model:** common Qwen checkpoint. **Data:** FourFilePermissionBinding-v1; 8,192 training, 2,048 selection, eight pilots of 256; permission pools of 160/32/64 assignments for training/selection/test, with every file–recipient cell represented. Test allocation balanced file, true-recipient and authorization labels.

**Procedure:** (1) Select the most error-producing format-compliant pilot. (2) Fit all linear candidates on original states from 4,874 correct and 3,318 incorrect training runs. (3) Freeze the validation-selected decoder and controls before generating and evaluating test problems.

### A.3 Recipient decoder on initial errors

**Target:** at least 90% among all initial errors, requiring 261/290 successes in this test. **Model:** common Qwen checkpoint. **Data:** synthetic_file_transfer_4x4_v1; 2,048 calibration, 4,096 fitting and 1,024 validation problems. (2) Fit 35 standardized multinomial logistic regressions on 3,260 correct and 836 incorrect runs. ### A.4 Eleven-head repair and preservation

**Target:** repair at least 30% of all original errors and change at most 3% of original correct decisions. **Model:** common Qwen checkpoint. **Data:** FT4x4-RowRepair-v1; 256 pilot problems evaluated under four presentations, 1,024 discovery, 512 validation and 1,200 test problems; seeded 128/128 development/test assignment pools.

**Procedure:** (1) Select the pilot presentation using donor coverage and authorization outcomes. (2) Enumerate all 23 nonidentity row permutations and choose the first correct donor lexicographically. (3) Rank heads by gradient-times-donor-difference, exact-test sparse candidates and select on independent validation. (4) Freeze heads, alignment and donor rules; evaluate originals, selected patches and controls. | Numerical execution | BF16 backbone; FP32 binary unembedding accumulation; fixed execution shape |

### A.5 Nine-head final-token repair and preservation

**Target:** the same coupled repair/preservation bounds. **Model:** common Qwen checkpoint. **Data:** SyntheticFileTransfer4x4-v1; eight pilots of 128, 384 discovery, 384 search and 768 validation problems.
